We -will wander hand in hand, While the hamlet, wrapt in slumber, With its little church dot') stand. In the quaint, old gabled houses, • Clos'd is ev'ry weary eye, And the watchman peers forth only; . •4-

From his steeple-turret high. Arm in arm then let us wander, Fear thou not, oh! maiden sweet, That yon good old man our secret To the gossips will repeat! L.-. Dere vas vot you call a maxim Dot I hear der odor day . : Und I wride id in mine album, ; ~.., So id don'd could got avay; Und I dells mine leedle Yawcob • He moost mind vot he's aboudt ; , "Tis too late to lock der shtable i....,.. ~ 'c- Vhen der horse he vas gone oudt."

Vhen. I see upon der corners Off der shtreets, most efry night, 4.• Der loafers und der hoodlums, Who do nix but slivear und fight, I says to mine Katrina: "Let us make home bright und gay; Ye had better lock der shtable, So our colts don'd got avay." Vhen you see dhose leedle urchins, Not mooch ofer knee-high tall, Shump riglidt into der melon patch, Shust owf der garden vall, Und vatch each reedle rashkell Ven he cooms back mit hees " Look oudt und lock your shtable, So your own nag don'd shkydoodle ! Vhen der young man at der counter - Vants to shpecgulate in shtocks, Und buys hees girl some timond rings, Und piles righdt oup der rocks, . Look oudt for dot young feller; Id vas safe enuff to say Dot der shtable id vas empty, Und der horse vas gone avay. Dhen dake Time by der fetlock; Don'd hurry droo life's courses; Rememper vot der poet says, "Life's but a shpan"—off horses; Der poy he vas der comin' man; • • AI., •••• Be careful vhile you may; Shust keep der shtable bolted, Und der horse don'd got avay. Why is a philanthropist like an old horse? Because he always stops at the sound of woe. He who is slowest in making a promise is apt to be the most faithful in the performance of it. A person once sent a note to a waggish friend for the loan of his noosepaper, and received in return krs friend's marriage certificate. A country editor thinks that :Columbus is net entitled -to much credit for discovering America, as the country is so large he could not well have missed it. There is a grocer up town who is said to be so mean that he was seen to catch a fly off his counter, hold him -up-by his hind legs, and brush the sugar off 'his feet. An Irishman who had blistered his fingers by en- deavouring to draw on a pair of boots. exclaimed: I shall never get them on at all, until I wear them a day or two." A lady of charitable disposition asked a tramp if she - could not assist him by mending his clothes. "Yes, madam," he said, "I have a button, and if you will sew 8 shirt on it I will be greatly obliged." The following announcement is copied verbatim from the original, which is still to be seen in the neighbour- hood of Bedford:—" Take Notic, aney purson Catch a Braken Thes fences shall bee procuted a Cording to -Loaw." I was never exactly buried alive," said an old clerk, recounting his experience, "but I once worked a week in a store that did not advertise. When I came out my head was almost as white as you now see it. Solitary -confinement did it." ' With most people the want of any well-defined system -or method is one of the chief causes of their getting be- hindhand with their work. A systematic method of working, combined with industry, will complete a vast amount of work in a day and finish it with ease; but without system and application, the worker may be in a -continual rush, and yet accomplish little. CLAMPING DOWN EARTHQUABES.—An ignorant Dutch- man, passing a number of railroad tracks in the course of a day's journey, and never having seen any before, was non-plussed to account for their use. At length, after -examining one of them for about twenty-five minutes, and scratching his head quite bald, he ejadulated, " Tey musht pe iron clamps, to keep der ertquakes from preak- ing up der road." DEFINITION OF A HUSDAND.—The English language is a copious one. If we had not previously been aware of tke fact, it would have been made evident to our under- etanding by reading the following paragraph in a Scotch paper:—" What is a husband? Hear a lady's definition. aHe is;' said she,-' a snarling, crusty, sullen, testy, fro- ward, cross, gruffy, moody, crabbed, snappish, tart, splenetic, surly, dry, brutish, fierce, morose, waspish, currish,'boorish, fretful, peevish, huffish, sulky, touchy, fractious, rugged,blustering, captious, ill-natured, rusty, churlish, growling, maundering, uppish, stern,-grating, frumpish, humorsome, envious dog in a manger, who neither-eats himself nor lets others eat 1'" Rimmious TOLERANCE.—Deacon Pettybone (to twenty- Tear-old son):- " James, you know my love of liberty, right of conscience, freedom of speech and worship; you -have heard me proclaim them in public time and time again. You seem to prefer the other church to our own, notwithstanding my arguments and persuasions. Well, this is a free country, you are a free citizen; far be it from me to coerce or influence you in any way. Go, my son, go; if your heart tells you you are seeking the riga path, GO. But if you do go, may Ibe struck deaf, dumb, and blind if I don't drive you from my house like a dog. I'll follow your path, and take from you all means of -earning an honest livelihood. I'll drive you to want e.nd crime, and die cursing you with my last breath. I -am determined to do my whole duty as a Christian."— Ifarper's Magazine. A merchant's wife recently gave him the following letter, with instructions that it should not be opened until he got to his place of business :—" I am forced to 'tell you something that I know will trouble you, but it is my duty to do so. lam deternained you shall know it, let the result be what it may. I have known for a week that this trial was coming, but kept it to myself until to-day, when it has reached a crisis, and I cannot keep it any longer. You must not censure me too harshly, fof you must reap the results as well as myself. Ido hope it won't crush you." Here he turned over to the next page, his hair slowly rising. "The flour is out. Please send me some this afternoon. I thought that by this method you would not forget it." The husband -telegraphed forthwith for a barrel of the best flour in the market to beisent to his home instanter. A NOVEL COUGH LOZENGE.—For a year past a pair of souls in Flushing, -Long Island, have been accustomed to share a thought between them, and twc devoted hearts have beat in such close and perfect unison as to produce 'but one rounded and complete throb. Now, alas! they do so no more forever, and all on account of a cough. Miss C— and herfance Mr. L— attended the sociable At the Baptist Church perlours recently, and were happy .as usual in eaeh other's society, except that Mr. L— was somewhat disturbedby a hacking cough with which 'Miss C— was suffering. When at last the sociable was over, and the pair started -on the three-quarter-mile lap to diss C--'s house—which, it being moonlight and not too late, it is safe to assume was not to be covered -too quickly—the lady was seized with a violent parox- ysm of coughing. In great distress, Mr. L— supported her tenderly' wishing he might cough for her, when a happy thought struck him. He always carried troches in his pocket; possibly one was about him then. A -quick search filled him with triumph. "Take this," he nressine it upon her; "it will give you relief, I am sure ;" and the young woman grarsfully put the small flat disc upon her tongue. They walked on. Miss C— sucked upon the troche and hung upon her lover's words, and one or the other acted so soothingly that her coughing spells were few and far between. Several times Mr. L---- inquired with solicitude if the troche were dissolved, receiving each time the assurance that it was not yet, coupled with the pleasing announcement that its efficacy was very apparent. There was a pro- longed and interesting farewell at the door, in which, for the time, both cough and remedy were forgotten. As Mr. L— moved away, however, his anxiety returned, and he called back, "Shall I leave another troche ?" And in the light of later events it struck Miss C— there was a mocking cadence in his to She lightly declined his offer, and entered the house. A few minutes after- wards, by the light of her bedroom lamn, a discovery took place which so aroused her indignation that in a moment Cupid fled, and before she slept the letter con- taining the fatal words "all is ovee was written. In his anxiety he had unwittingly given her a trousers button. " SOFT WIT.TE VEIN, BEErnam's Gurczatrut and CU- CUMBER "13 invainable for rendering the skin delicately soft, smooth, and white. A man who was very sick insisted that he was going to die. After his recovery they asked him if he really thought he was about to die. "I knew I was," he re- plied, with warmth. "Well," said a philosophic friend to an invalid, "had you a good Eright last night ?" "No; I never suffered so in all my life." " Hum ! That's bad! . But"—bright- ening up—"you know a bad night is better than no night at all:" Hearing a physician remark that a small blow would break the nose, our Daniel exclaimed, "Well, I donna 'bout that. I've given my nose a good many blows; and I've never broken it yet." By a quick movement, he avoided a blow on the head.

SLEHP ON THE 3 STAGE.—WhiIe Mr. Joseph Jefferson was once playing "Rip Van Winkle" at Chicago, he went to the:theatre very much exhausted by a long day's fishing on the lake. When the curtain rose on the third act it disclosed the white-haired Rip still deep in his 20 years' nap. Five, ten, twenty minutes passed, and he did not waken. The audience began to get impatient, and the prompter uneasy. The great actor doubtless knew what he was about, but this was carrying the "realistic" business too far. The fact was that all the time Jefferson was really sleeping the sleep of the just, or rather of the fisherman who had sat eight hours in the sun without getting a single bite. Finally the gallery became uproarious, and one of the " gods " wanted to know if there was going to be "nineteen years more of this snooze business." At thii point Jefferson began to snore. This decided the prompter, who opened a small trap beneath the stage, and began to prod Rip from be- low. The much-travelled comedian began to fumble in his pocket for an imaginary ticket, and muttered, drowsily," Going right through, 'ductor." The audience was transfixed with amazement at this entirely new reading, when Jefferson sat up, with a loud shriek, and evidently in agony. The exasperated prompter had "jabbed" him with a pin. The play went on -then— , with a rush.

How TO COM-POSE AN OVERTURE.—An extremely inte- resting letter of the great composer Rossini has recently come to light, from which we (Pall Mall Gazette) give a few extracts. In this characteristic epistle he furnishes a few hints for composing an overture, which may per- haps be useful to some of our musical readers. "First method—general and invariable rule—Never," writes Rossini, "compose your overture until the evening im- mediately preceding the first representation. Nothing inspires the imagination so much as necessity. My own best productions have been written while a copyist has been waiting at my elbow to take the piece away, bar by bar, and while the manager has stood beside me, stamp- ing and groaning with rage, in despair of ever beholding in time the desired overture. In my early days mana- gers always went bald at thirty! . . The overture to Gazza Ladra' was composed on the very day of its first representation. The manager relegated me to a small room at the top of the theatre Della Scala in Milan, under the guard of four scene-shifters, whose function it was to deliver my work in small instalments, as I produced it, to a number of copy- ists. These, after transcribing the score with all pos- sible haste, passed their copies on to the conductor, who immediately had it rehearsed by the orchestra. The barbarous scene-shifters were moreover instructed to throw me out of the window were no score forthcoming. Under such a method as this inspiration should come with surprising rapidity. . . . Second method—The overture to illiam Tell' was composed in a house overlooking the Boulevard Montmartre, at Paris. Both night and day the boulevard was the resort of all the worst scum of the city. The noise they made was sim- ply deafening. Nevertheless, I worked with desperation, and it was remarkable how seldom a sound seemed to reach me other than the exquisite melodies I was trying to give form to. Concentration of the mind is the secret of the success of this method. My last plan is not to make an overture at all. Meyerbeer did this both in The Huguenots' and Robert the Devil." It should be remembered that the above letter was addressed to a Signor Amaldi, whose nephew had been guilty of writing an opera, and who had had the brilliant notion to apply to the "Swan of Pezzaro" for ads ice as to how to compose an overture. The note concludes with "Best wishes for the future of your nephew, and many thanks for the delicious pate de foie gras you so kindly sent me."

How Ma. GLADSTONE TOOK THB Bum, BY Trtn HORNS. —Mr. Gladstone's visit to Tegernsee is a subject of great interest in Germany. The Germania, comparing him to Cincinnatus, publishes some reminiscences of former visits of the late Premier to "the most lovely of the Bavarian lakes," told by a personal friend of Mr. Glad- stone. "Formerly," says Herr von A., "Mr. Gladstone was very fond of climbing mountains, and I remember very well an ascent of the Wahlberg, on which occasion he was not behind the most nimble of us. He was dressed in the customary Alpine costume, and his live- liness and agility became proverbial in the little colony of strangers. On another occasion Mr. Gladstone and his family, accompanied by a party of friends, made a tour by omnibus to Fischbachau, Birkenstein, and Bay- rischzell. The tour being rather a long one for one day, we started very early from Tegernsee. Everything went on beautifully till we reached the well-known idyllic post-office near Miesbach. The high road winds at this place from Toelz-Tegernse to Miesbach down a steep in- cline, to rise again, equally sudden, at the other side of the narrow valley of the MangfalL Among the steep mountain sides and sudden precipices the road becomes s9metunes so narrow that it is impossible for two car- riages to pass each other, and in order to avoid inconve- nience niches have been hewn into the rocks, where one vehicle can wait till the other has passed. Numerous columns, characteristically named inartyr slabs in the jargon of the district, tell of the dangers i;ftlie road. Mr. Gladstone's party was at one part of this road in the greatest danger. After passing a sudden turn in the road, a herd of cattle, headed by an enormous bull, met the carriage. The bull, instead of going aside, obstinately waited just in front of the carriage, and the youthful herdsmen were unableto move him from where he had taken up his position. Nor was the driver's whip, which was vigorously applied to the bull's back, of any use, for instead of frightening the bull, the lashing excited the horses, which began to rear and shy till the situation became highly criticaL The ladies shrieked, and were about to jump out of the carriage, when at the last mo- ment Mr. Gladstone jumped down, took one of the wraps, approached the bull sideways, and threw the blanket over the animal's head. The surprised bull stood motion- less, and allowed a rope to be tied round his horns and his feet to be tethered. Obedient as a lamb he followed his leader, who led him back to a less narrow part of the i.road, the whole herd following close behind. The road was free, and without further disaster the tour was con- cluded. Mr. Gladstone was, of course, greatly compli- mented and congratulated for his presence of mind and his energetic action, of which, however, he would not hear, and dismissed the subject smilingly with a few words to an intimate German friend, with whom he walked the rest of the mountain. Never mind; . was the same with this fellow as it is with John Bull. You must catch him by the horns if you want to over- power him.' Many a time," concludes the writer, "I have remembered Mr. Gladstone's words, 'You must catch him by the horns if you want to overpower him,' when afterwards I watched the remarkable statesman taking a leading part in Albion's political events. Is the English ex-Premier going to verify this remarkable say- ing once more? From all I know of him and his country- men, I verily believe that he will.—Pall Mall Gazette. Public Anatysts have submitted CADBURv'S UocoA. to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt.

Mr. Martin Seater, of Weston Colville, has sold his ram lamb, which obtained third prize at the Stowunarket Farmer's Club Show, to Lord Ellesmere, for 61gs. _ _

There is such an abundance of fruit in East Kent this \ year that many growers cannot realise more than 6d. per bushel for very fine plums, and are allowing them to rot on the trees. Such prices are unprecedented. The Shropshires belonging to Mr. J. Bowen-Jones were recently sold at Ensdon House, by Messrs. Lythall, Man- sell, and Walters. The highest prices were as follows : Shearling rams, Mr. Allen, 462-s.: Mr. Thomas, 32gs. The. ewes made from £2 104. to £4 15s. per head. Pleuro-pneumonia has just broken out among a large and valuable herd of Jersey cattle belonging to Sir Richard Sutton, of Benham Park, near Newbury. Atthe -Newbury- divisional petty sessions on Thursday an order was signed by the justices for the slaughter of several of the animals. Sheep farming is said to have revived so materially during the past few months in Western America that farmers in the corn-growing districts, who were almost giving their sheep away for nothing last year are now likely to buy them back again at a heavy advance in price. _

A young horse may be full grown and as swift and strong as an older one, but his muscles and the ligaments that hold the bones together at the joints are like those of a young chicken. They cannot stand much continu- ous strain upon them without injury. Many young horses are injured by over-work, and their owners never know the cause of the injury. KEEPING BUTTER FRESIL—Never put the butter itself into wate:. Put the butter-dish into a shallow vessel, such as a soup plate, in which cold water mixed with common salt has been put. Cover the dish (but not the vessel containing the water) with a flower pot; keep it in a cool place, and change the salt and water often, and there will be no trouble with the butter. "Why a flower pot ?" some may ask. Because there is a hole in it; a basin, or anything that excluded the air, would.not do.
A FARMER ON THE USES OF Snows.—.An East-Lothian

farmer, who recently attended the show at Crieff; appears to have been struck with the remarkable merit displayed by the stock of that district. He concludes a communi- cation by expressing the belief that the large national exhibitions cannot index the general stock of the coun- try so well as district shows. The expenses deter many exhibitors from sending animals to the national show- yards, but no such obstacle or risk interfere with local competitions. He specially refers to Perthshire as a county in which farmers have derived great benefit from district shows, and observes that the agricultural de- pression, which no district has escaped, has not materi- ally weakened the enterprise of farmers. He commer.ids the practice of farmers and their landlords ,competing together. It is only by farming a good deal of their own land, he thinks, that proprietors can be thoroughly con- vinced of the real depreciation in the value of land caused by the free competition with the world's produce. PRICE OF FRENCH BUTTER.-According to the Gazette Coninserciale, the price of butter in France has been so seriously reduced that, following as it does upon the lowering of the price of wheat, the farmers are threatened with absolute ruin. The principal cause of the depre- ciated value is said to be the Franco-Belgian treaty of October 31, 1881, under which the import duty on foreign salt butter has been reduced from 12s. to is. 7d. per quintal (rather more than 2201b5.), while the duty on fresh butter, which formerly stood at 10s. 4d, has been entirely abolished. Other countries besides Belgium have claimed the most favoured nation treatment assured to them by clauses in their treaties; and the result is -that Belgium and Holland are supplying the markets of the north and east of France, while Italy is sending butter into the south. The exports of this commodity from France are falling as the imports rise, and the price at home has been lowered to the extent of as much as 4d. per lb., which means to a farmer producing 1,000 kilogr,s., or rather more than 2,0001b5., a loss of from £32 to £4O a year. No alteration can be made in the treaty until 1892, and meanwhile the farmers are bitterly com- plaining of it. FEEDING FOR For:K.-Some people may fancy that the subject of proper feeding is of little importance, and that any man who can handle a measure or shovel: can dole out feed to pigs just as well as a man who has paid attention to the subject of feeding. But such7a conclu- -sion would be very erroneous. Many pig-keepers are ignorant of the importance of right feeding, and do not exert themselves enough to understand the subject and be able to select and combine foods in the right propor- tions. They have got into habit of feeding maize to I hogs, and as this is a highly carbonaceous food, it pro- duces a minimum of lean meat and a maximum of lard. So long as the system of almost exclusive corn feeding continues, the product will be light hams and shoulders. Skimmed milk and buttermilk added to the corn will help to improve the feed.,-Wheat bran, shorts, middlings, peas, barley meal, &T., would make a still further im- provement. Then, if the hogs could have a goodfclover pasture to run in, dr even clover cut and given to them, it would be a further addition. These are all classed , among the albuminous foods, and help to balance the carbonaceous material of the corn. FEEDING HORSES.-Mr. Alfred Saunders, in his work on "Our Horses," gives the following instructions for feeding:-" As to quantity-the Shetland pony will re- quire a very different allowance from the Shire horse, and all the intermediate sizes will want proportionate quantities, supposing them all to be equally worked. As a general rule, the more good focd a horse can be got to digest well the more work he can do. The largest size dray horse at long hard work every day should get 181 b. of corn, 121 b. of roots, and 181 b. of hay, cut into chaff. 151 b. of corn and 101 b. of good meadow hay, with some roots on his resting days, is enough for the largest hunter in his hardest worked season. 151 b. of corn, 71b. of roots, and 101 b, of good meadow hay is enough for the ordinary-sized, hard-worked cab, coach, or omnibus horse, with more roots on Saturday night or whenever a little rest can be foreseen. 121 b of corn, 121 b. of roots, and 121 b. of clover hay is enough for the heavy farm horse at full work. The corn should be reduced to 61b. and the roots increased whenever short days and bad weather make the work short or irregular. Cut straw may also take the place of clover when the work is not Dressing. Good bright sweet straw, cut up and mixed with roots pulped, is better than musty hay at anytime. 10Ib, of corn, 71b. of roots, and 101 b, of hay are quite enough for light-worked carriage horses 15. hands high. When the work is very light, 51b. less corn, with 51b. more hay, with more roots should be given. If the work -is very light and irregular, the pace never very fast, no -long journeys, and the horses required to be very steady, 201 b. of good hay and 141 b.. of roots only may be given. Ponies and small horses must be fed in proportion to their size. They do better without corn than large horses will do. A child's pony should not have corn un- less its work is regular and fast. They will be more gentle and reliable without corn, but they should get some roots or grass with their hay. With hard-worked cart or plough horses one-third of the corn should be beans. Barley may take the place of oats with them if cheaper. Maize or wheat may form part of their food if all the hay or straw is cut into chaff and mixed with their corn. For hard-Worked hunters, omnibus, coach, or cab horses, about one-third of the corn may be beans, the rest had better be oats or barley, or both. For car- riage horses all the corn should be oats; beans are too stimulating for light work, and maize imparts an un- pleasant smell to the horses that eat it GREAT SALES OF SHORTIIORNS.-At Killhow, Cumber- land, on Thursday, nearly the whole of Mr. S. P. Foster's herd of Shorthorns was sold by auction, by Mr. Thorn- ton, of London. The prices realised were exceptionally high. Thirty heifers realised £2,492, or an average of £B3. Nine bulls realised £823, or an average of £9l. The total produce of the sale was thus £3,315, giving the high average of £B5. Amongst the principal lots were the following :-Oxford Duchess of Killhow Third, Mr. Titley, Leeds, 105 guineas; Royal Gwynne Fifth, Lord Bective, 70gs. ; Silver Surprise, by Duke of Ormskirk, Mr. W. Parkins, Blaithwaite, 70gs. ; Duchess of Killhow, calved November, 1885, sire Lord Rosebery, dam Duchess 123rd, was bought by the Duke of Devonshire for 505,g5.; Oxford Duchess of Killhow 9th, Mr. Blezard, Pool Park, Ruthin, 125g5., who also bought Winning. Beauty for 81gs. Sir W. Lawson presided at the luncheon held be- fore the sale.-A selection of seventy head of Sir Wilfrid Lawson's pure bred Shorthorns were sold on Friday, by Mr. Thornton, at Brayton Hall, near Maryport. The Brayton herd is about the largest and oldest in Cumber- land. For many years it has been famous for its dairy properties. The attendance was one of the largest known in the district at Shorthorn sales, and included commis- sioners from American breeders, as well as leading breeders in England, Scotland, and Wales. Mr. Getting, Buenos Ayres, bought Graceful Duchess 2nd for 66g5., Benson 31st 50gs., and Waterloo 43rd 55gs. Sir Charles Tempest gave 50gs. for the bull Baron Benson 16th. Mr. Cowx, Liverpool, paid 46gs. for Cumbrian Duke, and 33gs. for Regalia of Rhoda tribe. Mrs. Senhouse, Nether. hail, Maryport, bought several fine bulls and heifers, among them being Dalesman. 40gs. Captain Patrick, Stoneclough, Manchester, bought a considerable number of females at good prices, others going into Cheshire, Lancashire, and Scotland. The total realised by the seyenty head was 1,666 guineas.

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. THE CHATAUQUA CLUB AND POULTRY KEEPING. One of the most popular institutions in America is that known as the Chatauqua Club, which has been the means of disseminating a vast amount of valuable know- ledge, and of inducing English educational study on the part of those who have not the opportunities of improv- ing themselves in other ways. The system adopted is to issue to students a course of reading and work, for which very cheap text books are provided, written to facilitate home work. Papers are prepared after the course has been gone through, which sent to the head- quarters of the club are there examined and reported upon. There are thousands in America who have already or are now going through the course, and it is exercising a great influence for good amongst the more thoughtful and earnest of those who have not had great educational advantages. The enthusiasm which ani- mates the students is very great, and every year there are large camp meetings at Chatauqua Lake, where the system is discussed and improvements suggested. I Not only is the ordinary course of study engaged in, but special branches are taken up. Agriculture is very fully dealt with, and from what we have seen of the papers issued any young farmer going through with the course would obtain a first-rate education in the prin- ciples and theories of agriculture. But not merely these, for applying in his daily life the lessons he learns prac- tice and theory would be combined in a manner that would be simply impossible even in an agricultural col- lege. The following are specimens of the instruction given, which we print not merely to show the system, but for the sake of the instruction:—

130. Make the nest of a shallow box and place in it inverted sod or damp earth, and cover with cut hay or straw. Place nest in quiet corner, and place fresh, clean water and whole corn in reach of hen, but far enough away to compel her to leave the nest to get it.—Report breed of hen and eggs. Describe position of nest and how made. Report number and age of the eggs set and date set, also dates first chick and last chick hatched and total number hatched. Also how often the hen left her nest daily, especially the last seven days, and length of periods off the nest. If any eggs are broken, state the causes and dates. Report any, other facts about the daily progress of the work. 131. Place barrel on side, facing South-east, in dry and quiet part of yard or garden. Block up to prevent moving, and cover with old carpet or mat to shed rain. Fill bottom of barrel with dry soil to make inside level and cover with cut straw, hay, leaves, Sze. Sew listing around leg of hen and fasten this by a cord four feet long to the barrel. If a small yard can be easily* built in front of the barrel, make it, with lath or stakes; a board can be used for cover of the small yard, and to close front of barrel at night. Front of barrel should be closed securely, at any rate, every night. If any other kind of coop is more convenient, use it instead of bar- rel. Feed chicks first week with hard-boiled eggs, chopped fine, and bread and milk. After that, breakfast of well-cooked Indian meal, and dinner and supper of whole wheat and cracked corn.—Report date, age, num- ber, and breed of chicks, and weight of all. Describe the coop, size, and situation. Report weight of all at four weeks, eight weeks, and twelve weeks, with num- ber alive. Also weight of hen at beginning, and her weight when she refuses to cover her chicks. If any chicks are lost, report the cause if known, or describe circumstances. Report kind and cost of total feed used, and the retail selling price of boiling chickens in your nearest market.

132. Continue work described for No. 131, and let chicks run more freely. Feed oats and barley with warm breakfast of cooked meal, or meal and shorts, half each.—Report as for No. 131, and add date first fowls began to lay and report proportion of sexes in flocks.

133. Build small lean-to hen-house with large window on south-east side to permit sunshine to reach floor. Floor should be loose gravel. If on the ground, gravel three inches deep. If board floor, cover with gravel or sand one or two inches deep. For heavy breeds use low roosts, not over two feet from the floor. Have square roosting bar, with a groove in the upper side. Keep the groove wet with kerosene. For nests, shallow boxes filled with earth or coal ashes, that can be easily emptied and cleaned. Keep dry earth, sand, or coal ashes under the roosts, and clean well every morning. Feed rather light; same as for 132.—Report number and breed at date of start. Report number of eggs laid in four or six months. Keep exact amount of eggs laid, and dates; also exact account of kind, quantity, and cost of all food used. Give weight of the whole flock at beginning and end of trial, to know whether there is loss or gain of flesh, and how much. If any fowls are lost, state facts in full.

134. Keep in rather dark house with gravel floor. Feed breakfast, cooked Indian meal. Dinner, ground cooked barley or whole corn. Supper, whole corn. Re- move all uneaten food. A little chopped cabbage or onions, celery tops or green grass, will help the appetite. —Report number, breed, age, and total weight of chicks at beginning. Report total weight same day every week for four weeks. Report total weight and number of fowls when ready for market. Report kind, quantity, and cosrof food, and calculate the cost per pound of in- crease in weight. Report selling price in nearest market. If fowls are dressed for market give light weight and dressed weight, and describe how dressed. 135. Every incubator must be managed according to its own construction. Follow the directions furnished with the one you use.—Report name of maker cf incu- bator. Report temperature in machine three times each day and also outside temperature at 7 a.m. See Observa- tory No. 1. Report date and number of eggs at start, where they came from and what you know about them. Report date of first hatching, number of infertile eggs, and number of chicks hatched. State capacity of incu- bator and quantity of oil used. GENERAL NOTES.—In all above works, always have plenty of clean water in reach of chicks and fowls; change it often enough to keep fresh.—Report Obser- vatory work at same time with all above work, the more complete the better. It will be found that poultry keep- ing and the weather are closely connected. If you have no good book or regular paper on poultry keeping, ask The Question Box about one. The Question Box is here at Houghton Farm. Apply to it for any directions needed.

THE REPORT.—Keep a full and accurate record of all facts, with dates from the beginning of the work to the end. When the work is done, make up your final re- port; get in all the facts. Then make a neat copy of it, on letter sized paper. Use half sheets and write only on one side. Date the report and sign it with your full name and mail it to the Club Headquarters, before the tenth day of December, and as much sooner as you please. It will be noticed that one or the strong features of this system is not only that instruction is given, but the results are all to be reported. Telling how to do a thing is all very well, but no good is done unless the knowledge imparted is applied, and this method happily secures that every one shall show how he has used the information. We commend this to those who are en- gaged in teaching, and we wish a scheme could be de- vised by which the same work could be done in this country

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

CABBAGE.—Favoured by suitable weather, these, though sown on the same day of the month, are in ad- vance of previous years. If the ground where it is in- tended to plant them is not ready, the largest plants should be taken out at once and pricked in a bed a few inches distant, and the smaller ones still nearer. At planting time leave a plant every foot distant either way, and place some earth round the stems, and the probabili- ties are that they will be two or three weeks in advance of those taken out, especially if some manure has been forked into the bed. FRONT GARDEN.—Herbaceous Phloxes are now very gay in the beds and borders, as are also Gladioli that have remained in the ground all winter, as well as those planted out in the spring. The best Phloxes are those that were transplanted two years ago, and it is advisable to take up some portion of the stock annually, and re- plant, if only a foot or two distant from where the original clump was. Unless well fed the plants exhaust the soil, so that this operation is imperative.—Myosotis (Forget-me-Not) : When these plants are allowed to re- main after they have flowered to mature their seed, numbers of seedlings will be seen in all directions, which, if taken up and pricked in circular patches, six inches distant, and every other plant of these taken up in spring to plant elsewhere, a prolonged season of flowering may be expected. THE GREENHOUSE.—The present is a fittirig time to give this structure a good cleaning out by washing all the woodwork and the glass if dirty, as well as lime- washing all such parts that require it. If the house is heated by a flue, it should be cleaned. The boiler also requires similar attention, and if the water has been in it and the pipes all the summer, it should be emptied and then filled with clean water, which circulates with greater ease and celerity than that loaded with corrosive particles. After everything has been overhauled, light a fire to see if matters are all right, and in readiness to dispel damp or exclude frost. When the plants are re- introduced wash all the pots, and arrange them as much for the welfare of the plants as general appearance and effect. Let those that dislike the rays of the sun occupy a shady part of the house, and use similar discretion with sun-loving plants. Greenhouse plants now in flower are the following :—Heliotrope, Liliums, Fuchsias, Balsams, Scarboro' Lily, Tuberose Begonias, &c. GATHERING FRITIT.—It is not easy to specify any time at which apples and pears should be picked, as soil and positions of neighbouring gardens differ so much as to influence crops more than in those situated some miles distant. Fortunately there is one good rule to go by that is applicable to every locality, and that is to cut the fruit, —say, two or three as dissimilar as possible—of each tree, and if the pips or seed are changing their colour from white to brown they may safely be gathered. Pro- bably the smaller specimen examined may have not reached that stage. Those like it should therefore be left on the tree for a week or ten days later. It is a mis- take to suppose that because a few fruit are ready the others must be so. With early varieties, however—and it is of these we write now—the interval between the first ripe fruit and the last is not so great as with later kinds, and the pips in these should be allowed to become quite brown before the fruit is gathered. Early pears, such as Jargonelle and Williams' Bon Chretion, if per- mitted to attain that state of maturity on the tree, would be what is termed" sleepy," or decayed, in less than a week alter being gathered. Apples are not quite so fickle, but they soon get flat in flavour if left too long on the trees. It should also be stated that it is useless to attempt to preserve either early apples or pears for many days after they are ripe. MISCELLANEOUS.—The propagatign of various bedding plants should be at once completed, and, if a cold frame or one on a slight hot-bed is available, all the better, as so many more kinds can be more successfully rooted. Verbenas, Salvias, Heliotrope, Petunias, Ageratums, and Lobelias enjoy slight warmth at this date. Instead of taking cuttings of the latter in the usual way, we pre- fer to take pieces with six or 12 shoots with roots at- tached, and pot in 3-in, pots, using for the purpose some light sandy soil. If kept close with Ulu cuttings for a week or ten days, they may be inured by placipg them where they can have more air. Pots five inches in diameter should be prepared for the others by filling them—after being well crocked—within an inch of the top, with a mixture of—Three loam, one leaf mould, and one-sixth sand. Over the drainage place some of the rougher portions of the soil or some half-decayed leaves, in older to prevent the fine particles of soil mixing with the crocks and obstructing the free passage of water. Press the soil moderately firm, and cover it over with half an inch of sand, sufficiently dry to trickle in to fill the hole round the cutting. The value of silver sand or good river sand is that it does not hold so much water between its particles as soil, and its importance to the gardener is such that it is indispensable to the rooting of some of our most delicate plants. It is of the utmost importance that the cuttings should not be allowed to flag, and immediately they are inserted they should have a gentle sprinkle overhead, and conveyed into the frame kept close and shaded from the sun until they have formed a few roots.

FACTION RIOT AT LIVERPOOL. A gathering of Social Democrats at Liverpool on Sunday caas.d some excitement at the south end of the city, endinv in a riot between Catho- lics and Orangemen. For some time the Catholic party have complained of their church and school windows being smashed by Orangemen, and Sunday afternoon the Orange volunteer band returning from church parade through the crowded streets were stoned and their instruments broken and damaged by Catholics, in return for similar treatment dealt out by Orangemen to them on Friday night. Many windows in Mill-street were riddled with stones, and the police arrested 13 of the ringleaders. For nearly three hours the neighbourhood was a scene of disorder.

A somewhat notorious canal-boat runner, Some years ago on the Mohawk, laid a wager that he could throw a half-witted, blustering fellow clear across that narrow river. The bet was taken, and the stakes placed in the holder's hands. A large crowd went to see the per- formance. The wag. with composure, seized the man by the nape of his neck and the " shock" of his breeches, and pitched him headlong about six feet into the river. Ha came out puffing and blowing like a porpoise, and sput- tered out, "You've lost your bet !" "Not by a jugfull !" replied his tormentor; I only want to get the 'heft' of you. I'll throw real all day, but what I'll get you over. When I bet, I bet to win !" The stakes were "drawn."

During the recent visit of the Princess Louisa to Bos- ton a very handsome little fellow staying at the same hotel, who was a general favourite among the guests, chanced to be in the hallway one morning when Her Royal Highness was passing on the way to her apart- ments. Fond of marble shooting, and having no one to play with just then, he politely asked the distinguished lady, whom he did not then know, to have a game with him. She was so pleased with the charming manner of the boy that she promptly accepted his invitation, and a little time was spent in jolly sport. In the course of the play the little chap learned that his fair antagonist was a person of very great importance, but her exact title passed quickly from his mind, if indeed he caught it at all. Afterwards, when his mamma asked him where he had been, he said, with a boastful shake of his head. "Oh, I've been playing marbles with the Queen of Sheba." SERIOUS CHARGE! AGAINST A MANCHESTER MINISTER.— At Manchester, on Monday, the Rev. James Mackie, minis- ter to the Scotch National Church, Bloomsbury, Manches- ter, was charged with assaulting John Carswell. an elder o.f the church. There have been disputes between the minister and the elders, arid about twelve months ago there were some magisterial proceedings arising out of the mode of making collections in the church. The complainant, in his evi- dence, said that he went to the vestry, and seeing Mr. Mackie make a movement as if he would seize the church officer, he stepped forward and said, You must not inter- fere with the officer in the performance of his duty." Mr. Mackie then said, "I'll soon du for you," and put his hand to his breast and drew out a weapon and struck him on the forehead, inflicting a wound from which blood flowed freely. —Otherevidencr showed that the minister was robed at the time of the alleged assault, and that the weapon he produced from under his coat was a butcher's steel, which was broken in the struggle —The case was adjourned, defendant being liberated OR his own recognisances.

WASTE.—The amount of preventible waste which takes place daily in our workshops is astopishing. It must never strike the minds of some of our workmen that every pennyworth of iron and steel entrusted to them to " manipulate " has to be paid for. They never consider that an inch or two of iron too much in the length of a bar can make any appreciable difference in the cost of the job on which they may be operating. Very true, it may not; but when we remember that there may be two or three hundred men in the same shop holding the same opinion, then it does make an appreciable difference, and a very great one, too, in the cost of the machinery made —or, rather, in the difference of the profit realised. They should also remember that it is from the profits alone that their wages have to be paid; and that the greater these profits can be made, the better chance they will have of sharing in them by receiving higher wages. The abuse of tools is another importanti item in workshop economy, and one that cannot be too bighlyreprehended. Take, for instance, files. How many mechanics in a thousand know how properly to use one? If it happens .to be entirely new, with good cutting powers it is rushed over the work as if the intention seemed' to be to make the file, and not the work, snaooth as quickly as possible. "Xis only a file, and doesn't cost much; be- sides, it can easily be re-cut." Oil and waste are materials that suffer greatly at the "hands" of improvi- dent and careless workmen. They not only oil the waste a great deal too much, but waste the oil in making it do duty for soap, water, and towel. Another source of loss is found in the want of careful firing—shovelling on coals when not needed. We remember an instance that oc- curred not very long ago in Oldham, which will fully illustrate our meaning. The fireman had got a full heaa of steam on, and everything seemed to be working satis- factory, when the " governor " happened to make his appearance in the fire-hole. Immediately the fireman caught sight of him he opened the furnace door, and afraid, as he thought, of being caught "doing nothing," commenced throwing the coals on to the fire as fast as he could. The "governor" looked at the steam gauge, saw how matters stood, and turning to the fireman, said: "How'd on, lad! Sit thee deawn again. Thou'd better do neawt at a' than shove coal in th' furnace when it's noan wanted !"—Michanical Progress.

div.head: FATUNE TELLING AT WARRING-
div.p: FATUNE TELLING AT WARRING-

TON. At the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, Mary Ellen Smith, a young married woman, Wes charged with being a rogue and a vagabond, and with having pretended to tell fortunes in the fair ground at Warrington on Monday. Mr. P. Davies • appeared for the defendant and pleaded not guilty. Chief Constable Hunt said he had recently received information from respectable persons in the town, employers of domestic servants and so forth, that there was a woman in the fair ground telling for- tunes to people who went there by the dozen. The prisoner, it was found, lived in one of the vans on the fair ground, and was in :the habit of hawking ' in a small way baskets and clothes pegs, and there ' was evidence to show that she offered these articles at a very low price, and then introduced the ;natter of fortune telling. The Chief Constable men- tioned that they had a number of witnesses pre- sent who were, however, somewhat reluctant to give evidence, and then called as a first witness ea prepossessing young female who, it was stated, was a greengrocer's assistant. She said that they bad heard a good deal of talk about the fortune telling on the market ground, and consequently her mis" tress sent her to see if there was anything in it. When she got to the fair ground about half-paA seven o'clock at night the prisoner beckoned to her/ and told her to kneel down behind a piece of can- vas, because if the "bobbies" saw them she (prisoner) would get six months and witness would get three. A little boy was also placed at the corner of the canvas to watch any one coming across the fair ground. There were seven or eight other young women kneeling down. Witness was asked to cut the cards, after which prisoner proceeded to tell her fortune. Witness was informed that she had blue eyes, and a young man who was light and fair. -She had had an offer of marriage and presents made 10 her, but there were other presents and very hand- some ones to come. She had been born -very luck)4 and, added prisoner, " You stand very lucky here, pointing to the cards. Witness was. also informed that she would be • married, and " veil soon, too ; " indeed much sooner than she Wao thinking of. She asked prisoner what the charge was, and the latter replied that was sixpence which she paid. The next witness called was a young married woman, who deposed that the prisoner had come to her house selling baskets and clothes pegs. The pegs were id. dozen, and she took a dozen. Prisoner then told witness that she had something on her mind which she could ease for her for a shilling. Witness at first said that she could not afford this, but on prisoner saying "You can, and you must," sbe agreed to pay the shilling. She was then told by the prisoner that she had not got her lot; she Icae not married to the man she ought to have married, but she would yet see the- man she ought to have had, and that before very long. He was a light man and tall, and witness was further told that sbe was lucky, and should have money, but no more children. In answer to Mr. Davies, this witness said she thought that the pri" Boner was a woman who could ease her mind, and she did not repent having paid the money. When asked why she thought the woman could ease her mind, she replied that it was because she had ono. before had her fortune told, and it came true. Other two young women were likewise called as witnesses. The first a these was told when she went to havO her fortune told that she was not doing so well as she would like to do, but she would do well in time if she would only wait. She was also told some- thing about a young man, but she did not pay any attention to that----;he did not take very much in- terest in it. (Laughter.) The other young woman, who is a fustian cutter, said she had heard the woman talked about in the workshop, and she went to the Fair Ground to have her fortune told. She was told that she would be well off in time and that she was going to be married to a dark young man who was away at present. This witness men- tioned that she paid 3d and the former one said sly; paid 6d. Inspector Spinks spoke to arresting Pri' soner in her van. He found there the three cards produced. There were about thirty or forty personS visited prisoner of a night, an he should think be had had fifty complaints of her.—Mr. Davies, in the course of his remarks in defence, said it was an nu' fortunate thing for such persons as the prisoner that there were women in Warrington or anywhtre else so abominably foolish as to do what the wit- nesses had done.—The Chairman (Major Litton) said the Bench were of opinion that the prisoner knew perfectly well she was breaking the law, and that the case had been clearly proved against her. She would consequently be fined -..e5 and costs, all £6 5s 6d, or in default of payment two months' limprisonment.

The division lists of the Oxford Local Examinations were issued on Wednesday morning. Six hundreel and terl senior candidates Passed, of whom 37 were placed in the first division, the head position being gained by a student from the Liverpool institute. 1,039 juniors passed, 135' being placed in the first division, the first two places being awarded to the Oxford High School. THE PRIME MINISTER AT ST. ALBA:M.—Lord Salisbnri on Wednesday opened a Conservative Club at St. Albans, and delivered a speech on political topics, He spoke of the division on Wednesday morning as one of the most remark' able in a party sense that had ever taken place, for every man belonging to to the Conservative party in the House of Commons either was in his place and voted or else ke was paired. Referring to Parliamentary obstruction as it now existed, he described it as an instrument of torture ar plied to the majority and the Government to induce theta by mere physical suffering to concede things upon wbiell the leaders of the obstruction had set their hearts, and Ile said if representative gdvernment were to go on tb.',9 instrument of torture could not be permitted survive. Proceeding to deal with the debate concluded, the Prime Minister asserted that had never made statements attributed to hint bi Mr. Gladstone on Monday night. For instancl. he bad never stated when he assumed office that there Wer, caMs, as he believed, where the judicial rents could not paid, or holdings in which the just rents would fall the judicial rent, and that the difference should be Maid; e up out of the public exchequer. He regretted to see a 1-11 9 • position on the part of Mr. Gladstone and others of . party to throw contempt on the wishes of the Governin,.`°' to create a peasant protirietary. The proposal was eriglo: ally Mr. Btight's, and when it was first made, twenty Yeiri'; ago, it was supported by many Conservatives, hirase_ among the number. In Ireland the old moorings had cut away, and a new anchorage was rcquired to secare order; and the only way they could get it was by roultip ing the small cultivators, whd would make sacrifices apu_ undergo struggles to maintain the security of the proper 7 on which they depended. The multiplication of sr" e. holdings in Ireland presented the only reasonable hope... obtaining that securit, that trarquilty, and that orosp tber.ab itY: t upon which depended the happiness of the people ot unhappy country.
BOWLING. HANDICAP:3 AT THE
LIBERAL CLUB.

On the afternoon of the 4th inst. the Club Com- mittee made arrangements for a bowling main at the Liberal Club, the members who frequented the green being handicapped with a view to giving them an equal chance. A number of prizes were offered, to compete for which a large number of players entered their names. After a pleasant afternoon's bowling the following were declared the prize winners, viz. ;-1, Mr. S. Dunbobbin, copper kettle; 2nd, Mr. Arthur Young, umbrella; 3, Mr. J. I Strange, dolly tub: 4, Mr. J. Bouchier, hat; 5, Mr. W Stephenson, silk handkerchief and tie; 6, Mr. J. Heywood, comb and brush, soap, &c.; 7, Mr. James Jennings, pound of tea; 8, Mr. S. Holland, 5 cwt. firewood: 9, Mr. James Sankey, purse; 10, Mr. Wm. Warburton, half pound tea; 11, Mr. H. Highley, 4 lb. currant loaf; 12, Mr. W. Gleave, pair of braces; 13, Mr. G. Strange. This handicap created so much interest and was so much enjoyed by the members that it was deter- mined to have another of a similar description. Several gentlemen kindlyvolunteered to give prizes, and arrangements were made for a contest, to be followed by a tea, to take place on Saturday after- noon last. Forty-five members entered, and, be- ing favoured with agreeably fine weather, the ,arrangements were carried through in the most suc- cessful manner. Some good games were witnessed, the result of which was that the following gentlemen were declared the prize winners, viz. :-1, /yin Jas. Sankey, Winwick-road, bowls and jack, given by Mr. W. Pierpoint ; 2, Mr, W. Pierpoint, a copper kettle; 3, Mr. J. Walker, bowls and jack; 4, Mr. T. Critchley, half-dozen knives and forks; 5, Mr. W. Stirrup, a goose; 6, Mr. R. Bennett, a carver and fork; 7 Mr. P. Langley, a leg of mutton;. 8, Mr. S. Dunbobin, handkerchief and tie; 9, Mr. W. Stephen- son, a hat; 10, Mr. W. Ford, box of cigars; 11, Mr. J. Jennings, comb, brush, and soap, &c. At seven O'clock those who had taken part in the handicap sat down to an excellent tea provided by Mr. and Mrs Mitchellrthe manager and manageress, in the large room of the club. Mr. T. Morris was afterwards called to the chair, and Mr. S. Barlow to the vice-chair. Mr. John Crosfield attended the meeting, and in response to the toast of his health, proposed by the chairman, and which was enthusi- astically honoured, made a short and stirring politi- cal address. Ile gave a brief account of his recent i experiences n a visit to Ireland, observing that the condition of the Irish tenantry in Kerry was very much worse than he could have been led to antici- pate. They. were rack-rented to such a degree and hampered in so many ways, and had so few chances of making a living, that he was not at all as- tonished that the people were discontented. He spoke to Conservative gentlemen who expressed themselves as indignant at the treatment of the Irish peasantry, and for his part he thought it was only necessary to make the people of this country made acquainted with the facts of the situation to lead them to insist upon a great change being made. As a means to a better state of things there should be a reform of the conditions on which holdings were tenanted, and an extension of self-government to Ireland. (Hear, hear.) He was persuaded that the Liberal party would be again united upon these questions when they had made themselves better ac- quainted with all the circumstances of the case, and in that event he had no doubt that the Liberal party would succeed in winning the seat in Warrington. Personally he had no desire to enter the House of Commons except as serving the interests of the Liberal party in Warrington, but if it was their wish that he should contest the seat again he was willing to do so again and again until victory was on their side. (Cheers.)—Other toasts were given, and during the evening short speeches were made by the Chairman; Councillors W. Pierpoint and J. 11. Fleming; Messrs. P. A. Roberts, J. Walker, S. Barlow, G. Plumpton, J..Albinson, and W. Stirrup. A special vote of thanks was tendered to the com- mittee Which had made the arrangements for the bowling, it being remarked that the handicap had been a " great success, and it was suggested that at the earliest opportunity there should be a billiard handicap for those members who were not in- terested in bowling. At intervals during the even- ing songs were given by Messrs. G. Wallington, S. Dunbobbin, and T. Fairclough. The proceedings, which were throughout of the most enjoyable char- acter, were brought to a close by toasting the health of the chairman and vice-chairman.

On Monday there was another bowling contest confined to those who had not won prizes, and had been thrown out in the first round of Saturday's contest. There were two prizes given, viz., a vase and stand given by Mr. T. Fairclough, Manchester, and bowls and jack given by Mr. J. Walker. The prizes were won by Mr. S. Holland and Mr. G. Beard, the former choosing the bowls after a closely con- tested•game with Mr. Joseph Albinson.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO THE EARL OF DALICEITH. The Earl of Dalkeith, eldest son of the Duke and Duchess of Buccleuch, met with a fatal accident on Friday afternoon. He was deerstalking in the Achnacarry Forest, at the seat of his uncle, Cameron of Lochiel, in Inverness-shire. He bad wounded a stag. Whilst running down a hill in pur- suit of it his foot slipped, and his rifle, which was loaded, struck against a stone, and went off, the bullet entering his left shoulder. Intelligence was sent to the castle te procure medical aid, and Dr. M'lntyre and his assistant were sent for. They proceeded thither with all speed, hat medical Assistance was of no avail, as the earl died in about an hour and 20 minutes thereafter of hemorrhage. Lori Dalkeith is succeeded in the title by his brother, Lord John Charles Scott, who was born in 1864, and who now becJmes heir to the dukedom of Buccleuch.
FOEEIGN NEWS.

THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. SoFrs., SATURDAY. - After the rising of the Sobranje a number of the deputies drew up a new address to Prince Alexander, in which his Highness is describ-d as one of the principal heroes of the revolution of the 18th Sept., 18S5, and the hope is expressed that the Prince will speedily re-

tarn to Bufpuria. Sone, St/4Day —The banquet given here last night was attended by a great number of deputies and by the princi- pal actors in the revolution. M. Padoelavoff, the Premier, and several other Ministers were also present. M. Stambu- loff, who is one of the Regents, admitted that Russia had de- livered Bulgaria from the Turkish yoke, but added that she must not interfere with Bulgarian independence, as in that case Bulgaria might eventually prove as dangerous to the Russian as she has been to the Turkish Empire. VIHNNA SUNDAY.-A telegram from POthrOlOCZyeki, OR the Russo:Galician frontier, announces that Duke Alexander of Oldenburg, the Russian candidate for the Bulgarian throne, passed through here yesterday on his way to Vienna. VIENNA, Mov.—According to information from Con- stantinople, the Porte, on the advice of England, Germany, and Austria, is making preparations for the occupation of Eastern Ronmelia in the event of Russia occupying Bel-

pea. MoTenev.—The Reply of the Bulgarian Govern- ment to the Ruseian Note demanding the postponement of the trial of the officers implicated in the plot against Prince Alexander was deliveree to the Russian diplomatic agent, a eopy being at the same time sent to the German and Austrian Consnle-General. The reply begins by stating that the Russian agency has been misled respecting the trial, whish will not take plate itninedietely. The date of the isetairy is not yet fixed. the persons implicated being scattered over the country. The Note proceeds to say the Government cannot stop the course of justice, and does not believe that the trial will jeopardise the peace of the Principality. On the other hand, it considers that Notes such as that pre' canted by the Russian agent might, if they became known, produce that very effect. SOFIA, WEDIMSDAY. -- The Russian Diplomatic Agent yesterday accepted the reply of the Bulgarian Goyernment, the passage stating that Netes such as that presented by the Russian Agent might if they became known jeopardise the tranquility of the country having been withdraws. The remainder of the reply was not modified. MILITARY OUTBREAK IN SPAIN. MADRID, MONDAIL—Late last ni ht two squadrons of cavalry and 200 infantry, quartered at the San Gil Barracks in this city, attempted a rising, and fired severed shots, wounding the sentinels. The rebels, accompanied by a large force of civilians, marched through the principal streets shouting "Long live the Republic !" "Loae live the Army !" and "Long live Spain !" The troops were immediately called out in pursuit of the rebels, who on their way met a brigadier and eoloael of artillery, both of whom were knocked down and killed. The rebels then marched on the Southern Railway, and on approaching some other bar- racks were fired on by the troeps. At the same time other forces came up, and after a short engagement the rebels, finding that their rising was not respended to, took to 1, light under cover of darkness. Many of the rebels, prin- cipally civilians, entered the Southern station, and taking possession of a train started towards) Alcala de Heneree. Others fled to the outskirts of Madrid. I Many of them have been arrested, including several officers. I Telegrams from the provinces report that all is quiet. Many of the fugitive rebels were captured by the troops in the outskirts of the city, and the others who escaped by train, finding that troops were prepared to stop them at ' Alcala station, returned in the train towards Madrid. It is I believed they have now taken to fight across the ceun- try. The streets of Madrid are crowded by persons quietly discussing the outbreak. Perfect tranquility prevails. Ma- drid has been proclaimed in a state of siege. MADRID, TERSDA Y.—Further details which have reached here from various points only go to show that the spirit of the rebellion of yesterday has been effectually broken. The rebel troops are in the greatest distress. They bitterly complain of having been misled by their officers, who afterwards abandoned then to their fate. Scores are sur- rendering themselves voluntarily at the different military posts and villages, all being thoroughly exkausted and cowed. All the newspapers this morning demand energetic measures against the Republicans, and that the leaders of the revolt shall be dealt with rigorously. All parties are united to help the Government in their task of maintaining order. MADRID. TUESDAY—It is stated that Brigadier General Villaeatnpa, the reported leader of the insurgents, has been dangerously wounded while biding in a village near Madrid. The pursuit is considered as having nearly ter-

sainted. MADRID, TRURSDIY.-officlsl telegrams from Noblejas, in the province of Toleda, state that the Civil Guard there have captured the reported leaders of the rebellion, Brigadier General Villacatnpa and a lieutenant. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR. PARIS, WEDNIOD,AY.—The latest deepatches from Made- gascar, received to-day, represent the relations between M. Lenayre de Vilers, the French Resident General at Antanan- arivo and the Hove Government as becoming more and more strained. There is, however, absolutely no truth in the re- ported departure of the French Resident General. HEAVY FLOODS IN INDIA. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—The heavy floods in Eastern and Central Bengal have been causing much anxiety during the last week. 'Telegrams received from up country, however, state that the Ganges is falling, so if the embankment stands t*o or three days longer the danger will probably be past for this .year. The reports from the eastern districts— Dacca, Mymenaingh, and Tipperah—tell of ceMtinuons rain and extensive floods, by which the crops are mcch damaged and the railway and telegraph services are frequently inter- rupted. In Behar there has also been an excessive rainfall which will reriously injure the indigo crops. AFFAIRS IN BURMAII —BRITISH TROOPS SUR- ROUNDED, RANGOON, SATURDAY.—The death of the Myentgein Prince seems to be beyond doubt. Several of his followers have come into Manelalay, and they declare that they saw his dead body. It is reported that the Myentzein Prince's two'sisters are about to surrender themselves to the authori- ties at Mandalay. Boh Schwaydah, an important insurgent leader in the Toung-Wargyee district, has made overtures for a surrender. RANGOON, MONDAY.—The recent engagement with Bosh- way's force, when Major Auchinlfpla was wounded, appears to have been a sharp repulse for us. News was telegraphed yesterday that the remainder of the column under Major Clements was shut in by insurgents at Taindah, on the western bank, aboat 10 miles to the north of the old fron- tier of Lower Burmah. As the garrison at Thayetmvo was not sufficiently strong to relieve them, 80 Europeans and 200 Sepovs, commanded by Colonel Nepean, left here yester- day evening by special train for Proms to relieve the be- sieged column. FRENCH INTERESTS IN EGYPT. Paws, Morroay. —Te "Journal des Debate" in an article on the Eastern question, declares that Russian in- fluence in Constantinople is on the increase, whereas that of Great Britain has diminished. The article points out the growing importance attached by the Sultan to the posses- sion of Egypt, and in conclusion says :—" The Egyptian question is neither a Turkish nor an English one, but in- terests the whole of Europe. It is of vital importlnce to France, and if in London they are sometimes tempted to forget that fact, the more reason exists why we in Paris should never tire of repeating it." THE NETHERLANDS. TIM HAGUE, MONDAY.—The States General were opened to-day. The Speech from the Throne, which was read by M. Reeanskeak, the Premier, stated that the relations of the Netherlands with all foreign Powers were of a most friendly character. The financial condition of the country, notwith- standing the fact that it had been affected by the recent commercial depression, was satisfactory, and there would be no necessity for any increase in taxation. PaRIIELL'S TENANTS' RELIEF BILL. Mr. PARNELL, in moving the second reading of his Tenants' Relief Bill, asserted that if the General Sleotion had resulted in a mandate against self-government for Iteland, it had also resulted in a mandate that this House of Cominens should do as much to remedy the grievances of Ireland as a Parliament of her own would, and, late as the season might be, the eeergies of a young and fresh Parlia- ment should be equal to the urgency of the occasion. The measure, he said, HES a temporary one to meet a temporary emergency, and applied only to the existing rent and that of next year, for though he feared that the fall in prices would be permanent he could not now prove it. Replying to anticipated objection, he pointed out that under the Arrears Act there bad been no difficulty in ascertaining the ' inability of the tenants to pay rent, and as to the power now possessed by the courts to stay evictions, he argued that this would not prevent the tenant! being involved in large liabilities for costs, so that it was necessary that the courts should be able to stay proceedings before decree. Arguing the question of fall in price!, he went in detail through the returns as to the principal products, contending that the fall all round was more than twenty per cent., and for this reason the Land Act of 1881 bad conferred no benefits on the tenants, who would have been better without the Act and with their old prices. Next he showed that the Land Courts were recognising this fall, inasmuch as their stan- dard of the reduction of rents had been 05 per cent, under the Poor Law valuation this year, whereas before the be- ginning of the veer it was 0 per cent above that valuation, and he went at year into the figures of evictions, which he predicted must, according to all precedent, increase in the incoming winter. (Cheers.) Mr. PENROSE Erreasetepn moved as an amendment to the second reading that it is not advisable at present to re- open the land question. He maintained that the bill would stave off finality, would ruin the landlords, and give a further inducement to tenants to continue their agi- tation and violeace in the hope of getting something more. Mr. C. E. Lavers, in seconding the rejection of the bill, dilated Upon the hardship to the landlords of re-opening the questions settled by the Land Act of 1881. Mr. Glans complained of the spirit shown by opponents to the bill, and appealed to the House to consider it on its merits. Mr. BARTLEY maintained that the bill would not prevent evictions, but would stereotype and extend the misery and poverty which already existed in Ireland, and would largely increase tenant right, which he considered mis- chievous. Mr. Proanwroer urged the Governmnet to accept tke bill as the best means of, counteracting the influence of the National League. The Solomon-GENERAL for IRELAND thought the bill would prejudge the inquiry the Government were about to make as regards prices. As to evictions, he showed that, though reliable as to totals, they did not diecrirninate as to their eircnmstances. Mr. GLADSTONE commented on the fact that the amend- ment had neither been moved nor seconded by the represen- tative of an Irish agricultural constituency, the seconder not being even an Irishman. The plain and eimple reason was that no such member could be found. The question of the mode of relief was different from the question whether a case for relief had arisen, the latter being the substantial question at present. It was said that the Arrears Bill was limited to holdings under a certain figure. The hon. and learned gentleman appeared to attach great importance to that distinction ; but the Government to which he belonged —(cheers)—had appointed a tribunal to inquire whether the judicial rents were too high or not—(cheers and laugh- ter)—and why was not that limit fixed for the Commission of Inquiry. If the hon. member told bins that the Land Act was to be indefinitely extended and expanded so as to have the Treasury made a creditor with respect to tens, or twenties, or hundreds of thousands of tenants in Ireland, he (Mr. Gladstone told him that he was reckoning without his host. (Cheers.) The Primo Minister himself, immedi- ately on assuming office, said there were cases,as he believed, where the judicial rents could not be paid. It was perfectly true he stated in what way the funds were to be found. (Laughter.) He stated they were to be found by drawing On the Exchequer of this country. That proposition, pre- maturely born, had already received its quietus—(Opposi- tion cheers and laughter)—and if the judicial rents were too high, it would not be out of the public exchequer that a the difference would be made up. THE APPROPRIATION. BILL. On the third reading of the Appropriation Bill there was a lengthened and discursive discassion.--Mr. C. LEWIS first brought forward the election disturbances at Derry, and moved an amendment demanding an inquiry into the con- duct of the resident magistrate and police.—Mr. Joni; MOR- LEY turned the tables on the hon. member with a diverting account of Mr. Lewis's own excitement on the election day. He assured the Heuse that the affair complained of was of the most trumpery description, and called for no furthe- inquiry than had Creed! been made.—The ATTORNEY- GSNERAL for IRELAND declined on his part to countenance the amendment; and Mr. SEXTON severely and satirically suggested an inquiry in which a judge should be on the bench and the hon. member for Derry in the dock. There was no disposition after this to press the amendment, but the Parnellites insisted on a division. As on a similar occasion last session, there was no one disposed to go into the lobby in support :of Mr. Lewis's amendment not even that honourable gentleman himself. In the circumstances Mr. Creraer was induced to go into the lobby to justify the division. Accordingly Mr. Akers Douglas, while announcing 237 votes against the amendment had to declare " the 'No ' to the left is one. The one voted "No" because the form in which the ques- tion was put was, "That the words proposed to be left out stand part of the question." The ayes were therefore against the amendment. The House having thus voted that the question under discussion should stand, there could be

no further amendment, and the diecussien proceeded nomi- nally on the question that the Appropriation Bill he read a third time. But as any question can be raised on this mo- tion, debate went on for some hours on other topics. Sal- vage laws were discussed by Major Beech ; there was a Conversation on the proposed Royal Commission on the Ordnance Department, in the coarse of which the Attorney- General resisted appeals to give the Coramission powers to indemnify witnesses; and there was a persistent demand made for the third time this session for lie unconditional release of Father Fahy. Mr. Shaw Lefevre joined the Parnellites in their demand, but the Government declined to advance on their previous declara- tions. Dr. Tanner created an unusual diversion towards the close of this debate. He addressed the House ap- parently under some irritation, occasioned by the fact that a number of the Conservatives had ostentatiously left the Mouse when he rose to speak, and he was checked repeatedly by the Speaker for not keeping to the question. Being at last required to resume his seat he informed the Speaker that he would leave the House, and suiting the action to the word, added, as he was going, that " it was no place for Irishmen, and he was disgusted with it." The Speaker and members of the House titet this observation with cries of "Order," whereupon the hen, member turned round and, making his final bow. said " Yes ; I say go." He then left the House. Mr. Cramer afterwards carried out the Intention expressed on the previous day to call attention to our foreign relations, and the desir- ability of guarantees being !given to Parliament neat it would not be committed without previous knowledge to any new policy in the East. The Chancellor of the Exchequer, who had awaited to answer Mr. Cremer, deprecated discussion of delicate questions of foreign policy and protested against Parliament superseding the Execu- tive. He thought Lord Salisbury should be trusted to act now in a manner to command the confidence of the leader of the Opposition sixes be had received that approval in the last Bulgarian crisis. He said the object of the Gov- ernment would be to maintain in an efficient form the con- cert of Europe with a view to maintain peace. Sir W. Lawson and Mr. Labouchere criticised the noble lord's statement, the latter contending that Parliament was left without a voice in the determination beforehand of the obligations incurred in the name of the country. This brought the prolonged debate on the Appropriation Bill to a close about nine o'clock, and that Bill having been sent up to the Lords, the House adjourned at ten minutes past , nine till Saturday. HOUSE OF LORDS.—WRDNESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at two o'clock, and for a quarter of an hour the House awaited the advent of the Appropriation Bill. Finding that it would not reach them for some time, their lordships adjourned until half-pest five o'clock ; and then indefinitely suspended the sitting pending the proceedings in the Commons. At twenty minutes to eleven o'clock the appropriation bill was brought up and read a first time. The House adjourned at a quarter to eleven until next day at a quarter-past four. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNIISDAT. The Speaker took the chair at 12-15. NOTICES AND QUESTIONS. This WES practically the closing day of the session as far as the House of Commons was concerned. The Chancellor of the Exchcquer an- nounced that at the close of the day's business there would be an adjournment till Saturday, when it was assumed, rather than made clear from his language, that the proroga- tion would take place. A number of notices were given for next Session, but none of such interest and importance as that given by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in answer to a question by Mr. Webster. Subject, he acid, to the changes in the Government intentions which events might bring about, it was the desire of the Ministry to ask the House at the commencement of next session to devote its continuous attention to considerable alterations and modifi- cations of its present method of conducting public business. Contrary to the usual custom on Wednesdaver, there were ,several questions put on this last opportunity to Ministers. The Postmaster-General, in answer to one of these put by Mr. Shaw Lefevre, gave an interesting account of the pro- gress of the revenue from telegrams since the sixpenny tariff was adopted. In the six months ending March last there was a loss to the revenue of £22,000, but in the cur- rent six months the loss had been decreasing. Latterly there has been an actual gain to the revenue, which at the close of the six months will, it is supposed, be large enough to overbalance the loss at the commencement of that period. The Home Secretary, while unable to give any information to Mr. Qgotrian respecting the arrival of gipsies at Hull, lamented, amid laughter, the imperfect protection of this country against "the landing of destitute and insanitary aliens." The Secretary to the Treasury, in a reply to Mr. Labouchere, appeared to justify the payment of £3OO per annum for the food of game iu Windsor Great Park and Forest as part of the costs, charges, and management ex- penses to which, by Act of Parliament, the income of the possessions and land revenues of the Crown may be applied.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at four o'cleok.
