With re- gard te the army, he informed the House that a scheme for the mobilisation of an army corps was being prepared, but " the necessary transport " had not been settled. He quoted statistic% to show that the militia was stronger than Lord Wemyss supposed ; and with regard to the volunteers, he said the Govevnment were considering the question of an increase of the capitation grant. "At the same time, the Government were bound to consider the interests of the tax- payer." The House adjourned until Saturday for the proroga- tion.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 25, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 25, 1886.
THE FATAL FIGIrr AT EARLES- TOWN.
PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

On Friday, at the Newton Town Hall, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, the young man William Campbell, employed as a collier at the Ram Pit, Haydock, and living in Legh-street, Earlestown, was charged with causing the death of Hannah Smith at Earlestown. The prosecution was conducted by Police Sergeant Commins, who stated that the prisoner was charged with causing the death of the deceased woman, who was 39 years of age, and who had cohabited with his father at 181, Legh-street, Earlestown, by striking her with a brick on the night of the 10th inst. The circumstances were somewhat as follows: On the night named the prisoner and his father, along with the deceased, were drinking in the Odd- fellows' Inn, Earlestown, up till about eleven o'clock. At that time his father and the &ceased returned to their own house, and between 11 and 12 o'clock the prisoner, who lodged in the same street, a few doors away from his father's house, entered his father's house,' and a quarrel arose between him and his father. They went to the street and fought there, and after fighting some time on the ground the prisoner got up, picked up a brick weighing about 51135., which he threw at his father, as he (the prisoner) stated. The brick struck deceased on the left groin, knocking her to the floor. After she had been raised up and Carried into the house, and put to bed, Dr. Mounsey was sent for, and he immedi- ately attended. He continued in attendance upon her up to her death, which occurred about 8-20 a.m. on the previous day (Thursday). He (P.S.Commins) had reported the matter to the Coroner, and the in- quest was pending. Under tde circumstances, he asked his worship to remand the prisoner for three days. The prisoner was remanded in custody. He did not apply for bail. THE INQUEST.—COMMITTAL FOR MAN- SLAUGHTER. The inquest on the body of the deceased woman, Hannah Smith, 39 years of age, was held at the Viaduct Inn, Earlestown, by Mr. S. - Brighouse, coroner, on Saturday. There was evidently a great deal of interest taken in the event, as a large crowd gathered outside and anxiously awaited the result Mr. F. Harwood was foreman of the jury. Super- intendent Weir representel the police. The Coroner, addressing the jury, said that after hearing the evidence it would be for them to say whether they considered that anyone was crimin- ally responsible for the death. William Campbell, collier, father of the prisoner, deposed that he was a widower, and lived at 181, Legh-street, the woman Hannah-Smith having lived with him as his wife. She was a married woman, her husbatid, Daniel Sntith, collier, at present living at Han ing's Wood Mill, near Kidsgrove, Stafford- shire.. She was 39 years of age. The prisoner was his son, a collier by occupation. He lived a few doors above his house. He first saw his son on the night of the 10th inst., between six and seven o'clock, in the New Market Inn. He came in whilst witnesk— there. Witness left the public- house first, and 'c the Oddfellows' Arms. He saw his son again at the latter •place—he had fol- lowed witness in. He left again about half-past ten, and reached home between eleven and twelve o'clock.—The Coroner: Did any quarrel take place between you and your son in either of these public-houses? No.—Did, he threaten to do anything to you in any of these houses? I said, "Come here, William, I want to speak to you," but he made use of an oath.—Then you did not talk with him? 'No.—When you got home on the Fri- day night, between • eleven and twelve, was this womanin the house? No, she was with me and had been all the time I was out.—Did any quarrel or conversation of any kind take place between your son and the deceased in the public-house? No. , When we got home my son Edward Campbell, who ' lives with me, was in the house, and Thomas Finch and the deceased accompanied me there. We were in the house about a quarter of an hour when my son William arrived. We were sat in the front room. When my son came in he said "I want you to have a drink with me," and I refused. We then began to talk about work, and we went outside.—,Before you went outside was any angry word spoken be- tween you and your son, or between you and Ihe woman? No. Why did you go outside with your son ? I cannot say. I was under the influence of drink. \But why did you go outside ? We went out quarrelling. When we got out.ide we quarrelled with each other, and struck each other. I threw him down, then Thomas Finch came and parted us, but we got together again., I fell, and my son fell on top of me, and the woman struck at him.—Did you see your son William throw anything at you or anyone else? No. Nor did I see the deceased receive a blow from anything, but I saw her fall/ I was then standing three or four yards off.—How far was your son William standing from her? I cannot say, as it was dark.—How did the woman get into the house? I and Thomas Finch and another man carried her in. My son William came into the house again that night, but I did not see him. A doctor was called in between eleven and twelve. The woman was lying on the sofa.—Did your son say anything about the occurrence in your hearing? No. Nor on any day since.—Superintendent Weir: Were you and your son having a violent quarrel before you went out? No.—Was not your son orderQd out by you? Yes, I ordered him out. I ordered him out because he asked me to have some beer with him. He went out and I followed him.—Did you hear the woman scream when she fell? I did not hear her scream.—Has gyour son at any time struck the woman? Yes, once, about a fortnight before this occurrence, because she had been telling some tales about him. He struck her with his hand, when in the house, but I did not see him do it. He has not at any other time struck her. It is not true that two years ago he struck her and injured her. It was ber husband who struck her.—The Coroner: Have you ever seen your son do anything or heard him say anything which would lead you to think he had a spite against the woman? He did not like my living with the woman in the manner I was. The Coroner, addressing the prisoner, asked him if he had anything to ask the witness. Prisoner : said he had not. A Juryman (to witness) : Has your son in any- ' one's hearing ever threatened this woman? No.— When you carried the woman into the house did ' she say what she had been struck with, or who had done it? She said she had been struck with a . brick, but did not say in my hearing who had done it. Edward Campbell, a boy about 15 years of age, son of the previous witness, said he remembered the night on which Hannah Smith was injured. He went as far as Viaduct-street with his father and deceased. They went up Legh-street, and he turned up Viaduct-street. He saw his father again at the Oddfellows' Arms about 9 o'clock, witneos having gone there for the key of the house. Hannah Smith was with his father. His brother William was in the public-house, but not in the same room. He got the key and went home. His father with Hannah Smith and Thomas Finch came home about half-past eleven. His brother William came in about 10 minutes afterwards. His father and brother went out of the house about 10 minutes later. Whilst in the house his brother wanted his father to have a drink, but his father said he did not want a drink, as he could pay for it if he wanted one. His brother also asked the deceased if she would have a drink, but she said he must ask his father. There was no quarrel. He went out about five minutes after his father and brother. He went outside because he heard a quarrel. When he got outside his father and brother were standing up between their house and Lowe's. Finch was then trying to stop them from quarrelling. Hannah Smith stood about a yard away. His brother got his father down and fell on the top of him. He tore his father's trousers and scratched his nose. The prisoner got up and went round Roberts's corner, and came back again. A brick then struck the deceased, who immediately fell. Just before she wits hit she was talking to a neighbour named Roberts, who was looking out of a bed- room window. The brick struck her some- where on the left side.—The Coroner: Did you see who threw the brick? Yes. My brother William threw the brick; it had just left his hand when I saw it. He was standing, about live or six yards off.—lmmediately after did you pick up the brick which had hit the deceased? Yes, after she was carried into the house.—Did you afterwards give the brick (produced) to P.C. Lloyd'? Yes,.. on the 16th inst.—When the deceased fell what became of your brother William? He went away quickly, and entered the house where he lives. He did not see the deceased strike his brother on the night in question, nor did he hear her say anything to vex him.—Superintendent Weir: Did you see more than one brick thrown? Yes, another brick I was thrown. It was thrown before the one pro- duced, and was also thrown by his brother William. The first one did not hit anyone. When the first brick was thrown deceased was standing about four yards off, and his father was standing close by where it fell. The Coroner (to prisoner); You be beard what

div.head: PRESESTATION ADDRESSES TO SCHOOL INSPECTORS.
div.p: PRESESTATION ADDRESSES TO SCHOOL INSPECTORS.

It is intended, we understand, by the tallool teachers of the Warrington, Liverpool. and St. liel ns district to present addresses to Mr. Coward and er. Glover, late inspectors of schools in the district. The former gentleman has been appointed senior inspec- tor of the north-western district of England, of which the centre is Manchester. The latter is now sub. inspector, and is with Mr. Coward. The illuminated addressee will be presented at Southport or Liverpool to Mr. Coward on his return from the Continent. Mr. John Dewhurst, of the Parochial Schools, Warring- ton, has been chosen by the committee to make the presentation, and it is expected that all the teachers of the district will be present to say "Good-bye" to gentlemen who have won the esteem of all who know them.

The address to Mr. Coward is in a beautifully-embossed leather frame. It opens with two felding doors, with extra gilt binges, and on a mirror let in each door are passion flowers, beautifully painted in oils. The address reads as follows; I—" W. Scott Coward, Esq., H.M. Inspector of Schools, Warn ngton District.—Dear cangratu- dating you upon your well-earned promotion to the Senior Inepectorate, we regret that with this change ends your more immediate and personal connection with us; a connec- tion which, throughout the whole of the fifteen years you have held the office, has been marked by the most genial courtesy and .kindly recogni- tion of all honest effort on the part of those placed under your supervision. Your honourable devotion to the interests of the Education Department, evi- denced by your exactitude to the minutest details of the work, linked with your intelligent conception of the code. has not only raised the educational tone throughout your district, but has done much to broaden the basis of national education and to make it a living power in the State. Pos- sessing and importing into the work as you have done the innate genius of teaching, an intense sympathy with chil- dren' and rare natural refinement, combined with a keen estimate of cheractcr, a quick recog- nition of moral worth and great tact, you have placed the profession on a very high standpoint, and by dint of asso- ciation and example have to striven to purify the aim and fire the zeal of the teachers as to make the work to thews as it unquestionably is to you—a work of love. We trust that you may have a happy and useful future, and that while retaining our heartiest good wishes you may gain from the teachers in your extended district a rrpetition of all the good feeling which has prompted this expression.—We remain, dear sir, on behalf of the teachers, yours faithfully, T. WALBANIC (secretary). Joarc DERIILTBST (treasurer)." The address to Mr. Glover is also bound in an embossed leather frame, and reads as follows : • Thomas Glover, Eq.—Dear Sir,—We, the teachers of the Warrington dis- trict, gladly avail ourselves of the opportunity which your well-merited official promotion gives us of offering you our heartiest good wishes, regretting as we do at the same time that with this change of office ends the very harmonious and cordial connection which has existed between us for the past 15 years. Your great natural aptitude for dealine. with children, coupled with much urbanity of man- ner, inspired them with a very happy confidence in you, while from your pleasant accessibility , and honest consideration of the difficulties of I the teachers' 'work accrued a sense of lively sympathy for them on your part. Your zeal for the interests of the Education Department was folly exemplified by the just conduct of your examinations, characterized as they were by hard work, care in the most trivial points, and compre- hensive thoroughness, while your pronounced recognition of moral training raised it above every other educational consideration. We trust that you may long be spared to carry on your work in your new sphere of labour, and that the pleasure of your promotion may be greatly enhanced by the knowledge of the general goodwill felt by us to you,— We are, dear sir, on behalf of the teachers, faithfully yours T. WALBANIC (secretary), JOHN DEWHURST (tree- surer)." The addresses have been on view in the window of Messrs. W. Woods and Son, jewellers, Sankey-street, War- rington.

----- IT was JOHN STUART MILL who first des- cribed the Tory party as " the stupid party.' Lord Beaconsfield attempted to remove the reproach by what he called " education' " but he found he had to deal with dull pupils, and the result is that the Tories are, as of old, "the stupid party." Ample proof of this is unhappily found in the rejection on Wed- nesday morning of Mr. Parnell's Tenant Relief Bill; and, nothing now being pro- vided for dealing during the ensuing winter with the deplorable condition of the Irish tenant farmers, we are left face to face with a mass of eviction processes which are to be carried out under conditions that will be a disgrace to our boasted civilization. As a concomitant of this bad business--a con- comitant which under the circumstances is inevitable—we shall have resistance to the law, outrages upon landlords and their minions, amounting in some parts of the country to the dimensions of civil war. It will be a repetition of th,- result of the rejec- tion on the part of the House of Lords of I the Compensation for Disturbance Bill. Lord Granville at that time solemnly warned their Lordships that if that Bill—the necessity and justice of which had been demonstrated-- were rejected, the Government could not answer for the preservation of peace. We know what followed—how the whole of Ire- land was aflame at the injustice which had been done, and how a new lease of life was given to the conspirators who were trading upon the neglect of Irish grievances by an English Parliament. But the Tories do not profit by experience—they are the stupid party. Last week we explained at some length the provisions of Mr. PARNELL'S moderate Bill; and this week we have to say, after reading Mr. PARNELL'S speech in its support, that he made out an unanswerable case. He showed that it was a temporary bill dealihg with a temporary emergency, ana that so far from introducing any new principle of legis- lation with regard to Ireland, the principal clause—the clause providing for the suspen- sion of eviction proceedings—was taken from the Arrears Act of 188 z. In answer to those who argued that it would be impossible for the Land Court to deal with the cases that would immediately arise under the bill, Mr. PARNELL adduced the incontrovertible fact that in bringing the Arrears Act into opera- tion the Land Commission determined, in a few months, over too,ooo cases of tenants inability to pay their rents. It is not sug- gested that there would be anything like the same work for the Land Court at the present time. Indeed, Mr. DILLON affitmed that if the bill became law not more than 20,000 cases—that is one-fifth of the original num- ber—would require to be adjudicated upon. The Government contend that they can do nothing until they have the re- port of the Land Commission which they have instituted ; but, meantime, what is to become of the poor wretches who are being turned out of house and harbour? Poor wretches indeed! when there are no less than 400,000 tenants trying to exist Oil miserable little holdings, the rent of which is

below fifty-six shillings per year. Such a statement seems incredible; but it was made, Without challenge, by Mr. PARNELL, whose Point was that, when ejectment proceedings Were instituted, the costs of ejectment in these cases actually exceeded a year's rent. Can we wonder at the Irishman :showina himself rebellious who is turned out of the Mud cabin he has himself built, and driven off the bit of land—never large enough to keep him as he ought to live—which he has re- deemed from the stony hillside? He knows that whatever there is of value about the place is the outcome of his own labour; and that an eviction—when, from a fall of prices, he cannot pay the full rent—is the -landlord's legal way of robbing him of his tenant_right interest in the soil. Granted that an observation of this kind need not necessarily be confined to Ireland, and show us that English, or Scotch, or Welsh farmers are striving to keep the wolf from the door under such terribly hard conditions, and we will as readily say— " This .ought not to be; common humanity demands that the • State shall protect these I People." In the course of his speech, Mr. PARNELL ' quoted indisputable figures to show that the fall of prices was so great during the past few Years that the Irish tenant farmer was abso- lutely in a worse position now, under the Judicial rent, than he was when he had the old rent and the old prices. Now if this be 80, and no satisfactory attempt was made to impugn the accuracy of the member for Cork, it follows as a matter ot course that there is as sound a reason for State interference now ! as there was when the State stepped in and ; suspended evictions under the Arrears Act of' 1882. It was certainly pointed out by an op- Ponent of the bill that nothing had been t said as to the recent rise in the price of wool,l and this was thought to be a good point un- til Mr. JOHN MORLEY, on Tuesday night, quoted official returns to show that, while the value of stock and milk and its products was Over £30,000,000, the return for wool was only £327,000. Then, as to evictions and the Prospect of evictions, Mr. PARNELL disclosed What he truly described as "a very alarming state of affairs." He said : In the quarter ending the 31st March, 1886, a lo_eriod during which the right hon. member for A ewcastle-on-Tyne was Chief Secretary, there were Only 698 evictions, whereas in the quarter ending the 30th of June of this year, when the fate of the !And Bill and the Home Government Bill-for Ire- land had become absolutely certain, the evictions amounted to 1,309, being as nearly as possible double. (Hear, hear.) Then in the two months and a week which had elapsed since June 30, he found that there had been 1,037 families evicted, or ,311 souls. These figures were very alarming, and , they showed that landlords had commenced to evict. (Home Rule cheers.) If they had 1,309 fami- lies evicted in Ireland for the quarter ending Junef 1886, and probably 1,500 families evicted for the text oarter coming on, it would show for the last __quarter of the year 2,000 families evicted. (Home Itule cheers.) That would be higher, he thought, than .any quarter during the last 20 years. Mr. GLADSTONE, in announcing his inten- tion of voting for the bill, intimated that there Were one or two details which might be sub- ject to amendment ill Committee. He was en- tirely favourable to the principle of suspend- ing evictions, under conditions to be deter- Itnined by Parliament,. seeing that the Government, by their appointment of a Land Commission, had practically admitted that, in their judgment, there were some cases of in. ' qbility to pay rent. That admission involved the need to take action immediately for the Protection of the tenant. Replyina to the '
Ministerial " No " with which his arguments

Were met, Mr. GLADSTONE referred to Lord SALISBURY as having argued that, where the Teal and just rent fell below the judicial rent, the difference should be made up by the State. Lord R. CHURCHILL exclaimed that Lord SALISBURY "never said anything of the kind," upon which Mr. GLADSTONE effectively Silenced the Tory leader of the House of Commons by saying that notwithstanding his lordship's unlimited boldness in assertion, Lord SALISBURY'S statement was an historical fact. Mr. JOHN MORLEY pleaded for the bill in a forcible and sympathetic speech. He urged that, for the most part, the objections Which had been made to the measure were such as could be removed when the bill got into Committee; and entreated the Govern- ment, alike in the interests of landlord and tenant, not to throw away an opportunity of securing something like peace in Ireland dur- ing the autumn and winter. But he appealed in vain ; the stupid party are for the ,precent in the ascendant, and the bill was thrown out by a majorty of 95. "Thus bad begins, but 'Norse remains behind."

"A BILL to consolidate, simplify, and amend the law relating to Parliamentary elections" is the title of a measure which has been backed by Mr. G. HOWELL, Mr. PICKERSGILL, Mr. KENRICK.. and Mr. J. A. PicToN. As three out of the fourof these mem- bers of the House of Commons are working- men, the bill, as might be expected, affords evidence of an intentior; to agitate for a radical change in the law. It will be remem- bered that Mr. GLADSTONE, in formulating the Liberal programme last year, placed amendments in the registration law in the front rank; and the two General Elections Which have since been held have served to emphasise the necessity for something being (lone. We are glad to see that the new , 'Charter—for such it may be called—goes to the root of the matter by adopting manhood suffrage. Anything which stops short of that must be unsatisfactory and illogical. We are gradually ridding ourselves,, of property quali- fications of all kinds, and there is no need to attach a rating qualification to the exercise of the franchise. The citizen who is amen- able to laws should have a voice in making them, whether he is a lodger or a house- holder. Under the present "lodger fran- chise," there is a good deal of false swearing , going on at the present moment in our Re- vizion Courts, and that with a view to swelling the lists of voters. The standard of value is not, unfortunately, a fired standard; one Re- vising Barrister may place it high, and another may place it low; and it may thus happen, as has been the case at Warrington, that, from a change in the Revising Barrister, scores of lodgers who voted at the last Parliamentary election are struck off the list as being de- ficient in qualification. With manhood suf- frage as the basis, there would be no diffi- culty of this kind; it would be a question of age, not of the amount paid for apart- ments. Another principle which the measure carries out is that of "one man one vote." University elections would not be abolished, but those who voted for a University candi- date would not be permitted to vote for a borough, or county member. They would have the option of saying whether they would give a university, or borough, or county vote, as the case might be; but that is all the pri- vilege that would be given them. It is pro- posed that all the polls should take place on one day, so that the excitement, turmoil, and disturbance of business during an election contest would be greatly lessened. Bat on the other hand, the bill provides for a Far:
iL

liament being elected every three years—thus falling back upon one of the points of the People's Charter of half a century ago. It is not proposed that there should be payment of members. as was advocated in the old Chartist days, and as is done in the United States; but it is sought to throw a large proportion of election expenses upon the Consolidated Fund. and otherwise pave the way for the poorer class of the community becoming candidates, if they think fit, for seats in Parliament. The authors of the bill are determined to render elections as pure as possible, for they provide that on the day of election "all premises licensed for il the sale of intoxicating liquors by retail, and which are situated in the constituency in which such election takes place, shall be closed throughout the day, during and until the poll has closed." There are other provi- sions of the bill (such as that for reducin7 the residency qualification from twelve months to three months) which show that it has been carefully prepared, that it goes to the weak places in our present system, and that it is designed to place more power in the hands of the people. It is not to be expected that the measure will pass without modification; but as some such bill must be. passed before many years are over, politicians of all classes will be well employed in the meantime in discuss- ing its provisions.
"TOUCH AND GO." .

We commend to the attention of our readers a letter written by Alderman Bailey, of Manchester, on•the Ship Canal. it furnishes details of a scheme to enable working-men to become shareholders; and if there is as much enthusiasm in subscribing these shillings as there was in shouting for the bill, there should he no difficulty in finding the required capital in the specified time.

The bowling handicaps at the Warrington Liberal Club have been a great success. There was good weather, and a good green; the games were well contested, and the prizes were substantial and pretty numerous. There is to be a billiard handicap next, and as the club is fortunate in having five tables, it goes without saying that when the contest takes place there will be a lively time of it.

So the Tories of Warrington admit a Liberal gain of eight on the Parliamentary list of voters. Well. that is something—particularly as Liberals know that it is merely suggestive of the actual gain. Perhaps the Tories will see now how foolish it was to sneer at the Liberal agent being trusted to do his work without the aid of a solicitor. Mr. Roberts has done exceedingly well, and nobody knows this better than "our friends, the enemy."

There has been a young woman on the Warrington Fair Ground "telling tortunes ; " but she couldn't tell her own; she didn't know that she would be brought before the magistrates and be condemned as a rogue and a vagabond. People went to her, the Chief Constable said, by the dozen. Carly le said there were some thirty-five millions of people in these islands mostly fools; and some of them, of course, reside in Warrington.

It would seem that Falsehood as well as Truth springs Phoenix-like from its ashes. For the nine hundred and ninety-ninth time Mr. Gladstone has had to contradict the report that he has been received into the Romish Church. The latest statement, he says, "is the revival of a miserable falsehood, repro- duced from time to time, without a shadow of eviderce, and unworthy of notice, until it assumes a character very different from that of merely calumnious invention."

It is very gratifying to observe that the re- port of the Board of Trade upon the working of the Bankruptcy Act, which was issued on Wednesday, states that the amount of insol- vency brought under official review continues to diminish, that the average proportion of assets to liabilities continues to increase, and that the collection and distribution of assets is effected at a considerably lower percentage of cost than under the Act of 1169. Mr. Chamberlain does not prove to be all one's fancy painted him; but let us not forget that he gave us a good bankruptcy law. The election for the Widnes School Board takes place next month, and there is some prospect of a contest, as the Rev. George Bond, Vicar of Farnworth, intends, it is stated, to come forward as an independent candidate. It is understood that the Rev. J. W. Williams, Vicar of Widnes, will take the place of Mr. Brock, J.P., who is retiring from the work. Is it not possible that there may be too much of the clerical element on the Board? As a rule gentlemen of the white tie think more of their own Particular sect than of the interests of scholars as a whole. Let laymen keep a good look out, and mind what they are about.

Obstruction, Lord Salisbury says, has be- come "an instrument of torture ;" and a Tory journal states that it is the intention of the Government at a very early period of the next session of Parliament to invite atten- tion to a proposal for a very considerable alteration and modification of the rules of procedure. This means that the Tories want to extend the application of the closure. ' Let us at once admit that there is need for it; but what a howl there was against the iberals when they sought reform in this direction I At that time, Lord Randolph Churchill was the soul of obstruction; now he is the victim of it. " The gods are just, and of our pleasant vices make instruments to scourge us." On Tuesday night while Mr. Gladstone was speaking on I‘,lr. Parnell's Bill, he had occasion to iefer to Lord Salisbury's doctrine that where just rents fell below the judicial rents the difference should be made up oct of the public purse. As Lord Randolph Churchill, with characteristic impudence, ex- claimed—" nothing of the kind," whilst Mr. Gladstone was speaking, we give the pas- sage in question from Lord Salisbury's speech. It is as follows :—" But if it should , come out that the Courts have made blunders, and that there is that impossibility in any case of paying rent, I think it is not the landlords who should bear the loss. I think this would be one of the' cases for the appli- cation of the principle of purchase by the State, and that the State and not the landlords 'must suffer for the errors that have been made." It will be seen from this that Mr. Gladstone was right. Lord Randolph ought to apologise; but he wont—he is not a gentleman.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST WARRINGTON AND WID- NES CIRCUIT.— We understand that the Rev. J. Cal- vert intends leaving this circuit after the next con- ference, and that he has accepted an invitation to superintend the Manchester first circuit. rRINTING OF EVERY. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 25, 1886.
SUDDEN DEATH.—Mrs. Ann Prescott (26), wife of Mr. Thomas Prescott, of Halton •Vieve, Widnes, died audaenly on Thursday morning, after confinement. WESTON POINT CHURCH SCHOOL has been
tf,‘

and the result is eminently satisfactory. The cost has been defrayed from the proceeds of a recent bazaar. SHOP ROBBERIES AT RUNCORN.—On turday evening several petty shop robberies were committed in Runcorn, and, the thief being discovered, chase was given, but he

succeeded in making his escape. 12,1PROVEMENT OF DITTON Untitcx.—The interior of Dit- ton Church has recently been considerably improved. The pipes connected with the new beating apparatus,which wee laid on the floor of the church, have been put in the ground, and covered with fancy grids. SOUTH BANE BOWLING CLUB, RUNCORN.—After a Very successful seasai tide club closed with a tea at the South Bank Hotel on Thursday evening. About 30 sat down to an excellent repast provided by Mr. Jones. through the indefatigable exertions of Mr. Tom Saunders, the secretary, this club has a balance in hand of over £3.

DITTON WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—Anniverary services were held in connection with this chapel on Sunday. The lieu. J. Bryant, the newly-appointed Wesleyan minister to the Widnes circuit, preached morning and evening. There were good congregations, and the result 0; collections mad, in aid of the new harmonium fund was very satis- factory. ASSAULT ON A Wormittale.—Some of the men who recently struck work at the chemical works of Messrs. Mort, Sidi' 11, and company's chemical works, are allegcri to have attacked a labourer named Littlewocd, when he was leaving work at noon on Monday. It is said that he received rough treat- ment at the hands of two or three of the strikers, who de- camped on the appearance of the police. A RUNAWAY APPRENTICE.—MichaeI White, an appren- tice to Tnomas Hall, bootniaker, Mersey-road, Widnes, was summoned at the Petty Sessions, on Thursday, by Mr. Hall, for leaving his employment before his indentures had been served. Mr. Knowles represented the complainant, and de- fendant did not appear. It was stated that he was working in Bolton. An order was made for him to complete his apprenticeship. DRAUGHTS AT DITTON.—On Wednesday, a chess and draughts club was opened at Ditton, in the schools near Hough Ureen station, where the members propose to as- eemble each evening. Should it prove a successful way of passing spare time during the long whiter evenings, it is proposed to continue it until the end of March in next year. The club is under the presidency of the Vicar (the kw. C. W. WooII).

TREAT TO WORKNIEN AT RUNCORN.---The men recently employed in the building of the new premise: n Ckurch- street, Runcorn, for Mr. E. Irnison have 6een generously treated tq a day at the Liverpool Exhibition. Each mau also received two shillings towards the expenses of the visit. On their return the men all expressed their deep sense of gratitude to Mr. Imison for the pleasure afforded them by his kind liberality.

A YOUNG THIEF.—At Widnes Petty Segsions, on Thurs- day, a boy named John Fitzpatrick, eleven yesrs of age, was brought before Mr. Heald and Mr. GoFsage, on a charge of having, on Tuesday moraing, stolen 2a 4d,the property of his stepfather. who lives in Midwood-street. The lad took a canister that contained the money from the kitchen mar, tel-piece and disappeated. His stepfather found him about to take train to Liverpool. It was sta'ed that the boy re- fused to go to school, and that he, about a month ago, stole a pair of boots, which he pawned. The magistrates direc- ted that he should receive six strokes with a birch rod.

WASTING WATEL—At Widnes Petty Sessions, en Thurs- day, Horace Tyier, publican, Ann-street, was summoned by the Local Board for wilfully wasting water on the first in- stant. Mr. J. T. Allen. clerk to the Beard, prosecuted, and said that there had of late been considerable waste of water in the town, and the Board had resolved to punish the offende-s where they could be detected. The premises of the defendant were visited by an inspector on the morning id question, when it was found that a tap was running and had apparently been doing so all night. Defendant said that he was ignorant of the matter. The magistrates im- posed a fine of 23 6d and costs. For a similar offence, I. Percy, Sutton's-lane, was fined 5s and costs. A Mvstcrax IN DIFFICULTIES.—At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, a man named ganmel Gandy was brought up on remand on a charge of sleeping out on the 19th inst., he being without visible means of subsistence, and not giving a good account of himself. In answer to the magistrates' clerk, prisoner said that be used to live in Widnes, but had been an the road in search of work. When he slept out he only had a penny, which was not sufficient to procure lodgings. It was, he said, only a "sleeping out adventure." He was a musician by profession, but had not done anything for twelve months. His house was broken up. He did not play in the streets, nor in public-houses, but had been engaged as a siolinist in orchestras. Ihe magistrates allowed him to go.

dAME TRESPASS.—A man named Charles Russell was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday morn- ing, charged under two warrants with having, on the 30th of June, in 1884, been found coming from land at Sutton, where it was suspected he had been in search of game, with a gun in his possassson, and for having, on the same day. committed a trespass on land in the occupation of Mr. Geo. Gorst. P.S. Egerton (174) said that he was formerly , stationed at Sutton, and on the morning of the 30th June, 1884, be was on duty near to Mr. Gorst's farm, and saw pri- Honer and two other men on a field. Prisoner came on to the road, and witness searched him. He had a gua and a powder flask in his possession. In reply to prisoner witness I said that the gun was not loaded when he brought it to the police station. Prisoner, who expressed sorrow for what he "bad done, was fined 15s and costs, in all £2 17s 31. The money was paid. ALLEGED WIFE DESERTION AT RIINGNORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Peter Lowe, a flatman, tiring at Leinster-street, was summoned for deserting his wife, who applied for a maintenance order.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, appeared on behalf of the complainant, and Mr. Walker (Messrs. Bowden and Walker, Manchester,) re- present. d the defendant.—Mr. Browne said that that was the first case in that division under the new Act passed a few months ago by the Legislature, io order to enable a married womon to apply to their worships for an order of maintenance in case of desertioa.—The complainant and defendant, it was stated:, were married at Salford on the fits July, 1883, and, haying lived for a short time at Lynam, afterwards came Vs Runcorn. They did not live harmoni- ously together, and complainant had previnusly left the defendant for seven months. Since then it was alleged. ha had again illused her, and accordingly she wont to live with some friends at Lymm on the 31st ,Jaly. Mr. Brown produced a knotted rope with which, he said, defendant had threatened to beat complainant, and also stated that defendant had on one occasion thrown complain- ant's child out of bed, seizad her by the throat, sted at- tempted to thiettle her. He beat her to such a degree that her body was black for several days, an she was advised by a doctor, under whose charge she was,compelled to place herself, ta take proceedings. The defendant earned from £2 5s to £2 Ws per week. and Mr. Brown asked the Bench to make an order such as would keep .the complainant in the position she would occupy'as the defendant's wife.—Mr. Walker, in defence, said that the defendant would only be too glad to see his wife back if she would behave herself. He held that the Bench could not make an order under cir- cumstances -such as had been detailed. If so, it would be putting an engine into the hands of every wife to put her husband to considerable expense, and would constitute the Police Court a sort of Divorce Court, where a wife might manufacture a trumpery case for thecpurpose of getting an order against her husband.—Mr. Browne submitted that if he could prove cruelty on the part of the husband it would be sufficient to justify the Bench in making an order. He pointed out that the complainant had had to ask for the protection -f the police on more than one occasion.—The Bench held that a case of desertion had not been proved, and , dismissed the case.
SPLENDID TEE, 21. per lb. LAWLESS EROS., Market Place.—Advt.

THE VACANT LIVING AT Etr.. HELENS.-:—0010rie1 Gamble, Chairman of the trustees of the vacant living of St. Mary, the parish 'church of St. Helens, yesterday °morning received a communication from the Rev. Canon Eyre, vicar Of St. Michael's, Toxteth Park, Liverpool (who had been offered the living)., intimating that he had decided notto come to St. Helens. Ye) reasons for Canon Eyre's decision have been made public in St. Helens. The trustees meet again on Tuesday next. The living is worth £7OO a year and a house

WRITING ACADEMY FO R 'LADIES J-ND GENTLE- MEN NOW OPEN.—Smart and Company beg to an- nounce that their academy is open every Friday, at the Co-operative Hall, Warrington. Prospectuses to be had from Mr. Starkey, at theshop. A fine, bold, business style of writing guaranteed for one guinea. Book-keeping, by double entry. Smart's system is acknowledged by the leading London ac- countants to be the best. Proficiency guaranteed. Intending pupils are invited to call on Friday next. Pupils may be entered any Friday. Lessons date from time of entering. Time of attendance from '3 to 9 o'clock. Lesson, one hour. Academy, Co-opera- tive Hall, Sankey-street, Warrington.—Advt.

GENERAL ITNION OF CARPE'NTER4 AND JOINERS. —On Saturday afternoon a numerously attended , conference of delegates from the various lodges in , Liverpool and district, which includes Bt. Helens, , Warrington, Wigan, Southport, &c., was held at the: Branch Vaults, Liverpool, when questions seri- ously affecting the interests of the trade were dis- cussed, and arrangenients made far the holding of a series of meetings. to which both society .and non- society men will be invited. The objects of these meetings will be to explain the advantages to be derived from organisation and the easy terms upon which members can now be admitted into the above society; also to point out the evil effects that are . produced by the working of systematic overtime, piecework, and scamping, so prevalent at the pre- sent time, and further to consider if the time has not arrived when a united effort should be made to bring about a reduction, in the hours of labour to eight per day, so as to find employment for many connected with the trade who and it a hard struggle to procure the bare necessaries of life. The dele- gates present were both unanimous and determined to use every legitimate means to bring about an im- provement in the condition upon which the trade is now carried on.

! THE DIVISION.—In the division on Mr. Parnell's Tenants' Relief Bill the majority was , made up of 268 Conservatives and 31 Unionist Liberals, and the minority of 122 Liberals, one Unionist Liberal (Mr. J. W. Barclay), and Si Nationalists.

div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

-• -A.-- ACCIDENT AT WEST BANK.—The daughter of Mr. kin, of Church-street, West -Bank, was on Monday struck by a failing shutter, and received a severe scalp Wound. She was taken to a surgery and attended to at once. WELSII PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—On Saturday and Sunday the anniversary services in connection with this chapel were held, sermons being preached by the Revs. E. M. Jones, of Bagillt, and Francis Jones, of Abergele. There were large congregations and satisfactory collections. Poucis INSPECTION.—ThI annual inspection of the uni- form of the police in the Prescot Division, which includes Widnes and Woolton, was made on Wednesday morning, by Captain Ibbertson. assistant Chiet Constable. The books were also examined. Everything was found to be in a satisfactory condition. THE RECENT ACCIDENT AT HALEWOOD STATION. Charles Travis, the platelayer who was injureci by jumping off a goods train whilst in motion at Halewood station on the 4th lost, still lies in a critical state, and is deprived of the use of his mental faculties. On Saturday he was re- moved to the Southern Hospital. WIDNES BCIENCIS AND ART SCHOOL —At a meeting of students and masters, held in the science schoolroom, on Monday evening, the following syllabus for the ensuing session was arranged :—Monday: Elementary chemistry (theoretical), 7 to 8 , theoretical mechanics. 8-15 to 9-15. Tuesday : Advanc(d art. 5 to 9; art. 6 to 7-30 ; building construction, 7-45 to 8-45. Wednesday : Advanced chemis- try (theoretical), 7 to 8 ; practical chemistry, 8-15 to 9-15. Thursday: Advanced art, 5 to 9; art, 6 to 7.30; machine construction, 7-45 to 8-45. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.—Mr. S. H. Hartley has issued a notice to the ,ffect that the election of members to serve on the Widnes School Board for the ensuing three years will take place on the 23rd October. Tne number to be elected is eleven. It is stated the only one of the old members of the Church party who declines to stand again is Mr. John Br:ck, J.P., and that it has been arranged that the Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar of Widnes, should be invited to stand. The Rev. George Bond, vicar of Farn- worth, declares his intention of putting up as an indepen- dent candidate.

WELSH ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT WIDNES.—OR Sat- urday and Sunday anniversary services were held in con- nection with the Welsh Presbyterian Cnapel. The Rev. Francis Jones, of Abtrgele,occnpied the pulpit on Saturday evening, and on Sunday two serm.•ns were preached at both morning and evening services, one by Mr. Jones and one by the Rev. Morris Jones. of Bagilt. The sermons were most impressive, and were listened to by large congrega- tions, many being unable to secure seats on Sunday evening_ The collections were in aid of the chapel funds, and amounted to about £3.

CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROvEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.— The weekly meeting of this class was held on Friday even- ing last week, the Rev. George Wood deliv.ringa lecture on " Wesley and his Work." Mr. EL Randle (president) occu- pied the chair, and the vice-presidents present were Messrs. S. C. Beckett, and W. J. Shore. A vote of thanks was un- animously accorded to the lecturer on the inotion of Mr. 11. D. Kitto, seconded by Mr. J. Moulton. On the motion of Mr. A. Bibby, seconded by Mr. J. T. Nickson, and supported by Kr. S. C. Beckett, the names of the Revs. U. Wood and A. P. Wats9n were added to the list of vice-presi. dents.

FOOTBALL AT RUNCORIC—On Tuesday evening, on the ground of the Association Football Club, a match under Association rules was played between the Association team and Mr W Hughes's team. The game ended in a draw, each aide scoring a goal, The teams were :—Association : J Rhodes, goal; Jones and Rathbone, full backs; Stringer, Kendrick, and Henshall, half backs; G Hickson, T Smith, T Banks, W Steel, and J Nicholls, forwards. W Hughes's team: F Joule, goal; J Dean and P Riley, full backs: W Hughes, W Riley, and W Wright, half backs; T Abrams, H Hughes, R Wilcock, Wainwright, and J Barnes, for- wards.

AVEsLEYANIsAI AT WIDNES.—On Monday the quarterly meeting in connection with the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit was held in Lacey-street School. The local preachers met at three and the stewards at four, after which the delegates and between 80 and 100 friends were entertained to a repast by Mr. and Mrs. Stringer, to whom a cordial vote of thanks was ac.corded, on the motion of the stewards, supported by Messrs. We Hartland, W. Clarke, and Benjamin Brown. Afterwards a meeting was held for the transaction of circuit business, over which the Rev. R. Burdon presided. rho Rev. James Bryant was also present. The business of the meeting was of a routine character. 1.0.G.T.—0n Monday evening a fraternal visit was paid to the Hope of Appleton Lodge by several members of the Samaratan Lodge, who occupied the offices and entertained those present. The following was the programme :—Songe, "Only an armourbearer " and " Right men are wee ted," Brother Parker ; 'Jesus, I will trust Thee," " Behold Me standing at the door," and " Oh, won't you be a Christian while you're young," Brather Owens; reidings, "A tale worth telling," " Prevention," and " A saving wife," Bro. Coornbes ; recitation, "A little child shall lead them " and "Choose the right," Brother Parker ; "The little shoes" and another, Brother C. Webb; trio, " Crown Him," Bros. Owens, Parker, and Coombes. A vote of thanks was passed to the visitors on the motion bf Bro. T. Reay, seconded by Bro. T. Harrison, at the close of the proceedings. FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at the Arch Hotel, Widnes, respecting the death of George Edward Duggan, aged 25, who lived in lodgings at 2, Bridge-street, West Bank, and was employed as a labourer at Messrs. Bolton and Sons' Copper Works. On Saturday, the 11th inst., deceased was whitewashing the inside of the rood of a shed at the works, and the ladder he was using being too short, he placed it on a tub. Inasneoliately after he had got to the top it gave way, and he fell to the ground, alighting with his stomach on the ladder, which was turned up on its side. His stomach was much bruised, and one of his wrists sprained. He was assisted home, and attended by Dr. McLennan, but died from the injuries he had received. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." WIDNES ItIVISION COURT.—Mr. J. T.lFoard, barrister-at- law, who has been appointed to revise the lists of voters for the Widnes Parliamentary Division, will hold courts at the Police Court, Widnes, for the district of Widnes, Crouton, and Dittos, on the 7th, Bth, and 9th of October, commen- cing on the first day at six o'clock in the evening, and on the two following days at ten o'clock in the morning. He will also hold a court at Huyton, for the districts of Huy- ton-with-Roby, Tarbock, and Whiston, on the 6th proximo. All the new claims in the Widnes districts, with the excep- tion of those made by lodgers, have been objected to, the total number of objections being M. Tbese are divided as follows :—Objections to owners already on the register, north, 4; south. 8; new claims, north, 52; south, 27; occu- piers, north, 423; south, 279. Only 4 claims are made by lodgers in the south district, but there are 55 in the north.

RUNCORN FRER LIBRARY COMMITTEE.—On Monday the monthly meeting of this committee was held in the Commissioners' Board-room at the Town Hall. There were ' present—Messrs. F. A. Lake, W. J. Shore, T. Riley, G. Moss, E. Merwood, and J. D. Zones (librarian). Mr. F. A. Lake was reappointed chairman and Mr. G. Moss Tice- chairman. The following gentlemen were appointed mem- bers of the Hook Selection Committee :—Messrs. W. Hand- ley, G. Moss, E. Marwood, W. J. Shore, F. J. Norman, and F. A. Lake (chairman). The Librarian reported that 1,508 books had been issued from the Library during the month of August, being an inorease of 161 over the corre- sponding month of last year. The issues were classified ai follows :—Theology, 11; philosophy, 5; science and art, 51; history, biovraphy, and travel, 110: poetry and the drama, 5; f rose, fiction, 1,55; miscellaneous literature, 71. Mr. J. T. Brunner presented six Parliamentary returns. The Library receipts were Os 41. DEATH OF BE. BAGNALL.—On Wednesday the death oc- curred at his residence at 'Dunham Massey of Dr. S. F. Bagnall, formerly of Runcorn. Dr. Bagnall was the ,son of the late Rev. Samuel Baenall, M.A., for many years incum- bent of Weston Point. The deceased gentleman was about 40 years of age, and was educated at King's College, Lon- don. He was admitted a Licentiate of the Royal College of Physicians in 1867. In the tame year he was admitted a member of the Royal College of Surgeons, and a Licentiate of the Royal Society of Apothecaries. For some time he occupied the position of house surgeon at the Royal Infir- mary, Manchester. He was also senior house surgeon at the Preston infirmary, and senior mrdicel officer of the Gloucester County Asylum. Some years ago he set up in practice at Weston Point, and subsequently came to Run- corn. In the early part of 1885, his constitution be.e.ame impaired, and, in search of a milder air, he removed to Dun- ham Massey. His health. hcwever, was never completely restored, and about a fortnight ago he took to his bell. He was a skilful surgeon. WIDNES Penises CHURCH HARVEST FESTIVAL—A harvest thanksgiving service was held at St. Mary's Church, nes, on Thursday evening, 'when the sermon was preached by the Rev. G. 'Howell, of Liverpool, to a large congrega- tion. The decoration of the church had been in able hands, and the interior of the sacred building had a eery pleasing look. The words "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof" were prominently displayed as a motto. The font and communion were tastefully embellished with flowers and products of the field, and each window sill was similarly bedecked. Harvest decorations bung pendant from the gas standards, and various mottoes were suspended: on the walls. The preacher took for his text the words' " They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." The proces- sional hymn was the one commencing "Come, ye thankfnl people, come," and recessional hymn was the one beginning , with the words "Praise, oh praise, our God and king." 'The collection, which was in aid of a fund to carry out the painting of the interior of the church, realised nearly £4. The services are to be condoned on Sunday. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES. On Thursday, the re-opening of this church after renovation was celebrated by a tea and snecial service. The woodwork of the church, which is of pitchpine, has been re-yernished. and the walls have been painted silver grey. A gothic arch has been placed (wee the pulpit, and painted in different colours. The seats also have been re-varnished. The con• tractors for the work were Messrs. Philips and'Ray. Early in the evening a public tea was held in Mali's Temperance Hall, to which about 100 persons sat down. Amongst those present were the Revs. R. Yeatman. D. Davies, and Brad- shaw (Peasley Cross). The following ladies presided at the tables :—Miss Thomas, Miss Hurst, Mrs. W. Darning, Mrs. J. There was a good congrega- tion. The collections were in aid of the renovation fund. - During the time the church has been closed for renovation, service has been condacted in Mali's Temperance Hall.

div.head: WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB.

A general meeting of the members of this club was held on Thursday evening at the club-house, the Norton Arms. Dr. Richards was voted to the chair. He said that the sec- retary of the club (Mr. A. Brown) had called a general meeting of the members more its a custom than for the transaction ot any 'very particular business. There was nothing very impertant except that the members could receive copies of the balance sheet, and those who were desirous of getting cards could do so that evening by pay- ing their entrance fee. There was also the election of a second team captain, in the place of Mr. Stirrup, who was unfortunately obliged to resign that position. lie might also mention that the clothes of the playing members were to be given out on the night following at the Central Hotel.— Mr. Pilling proposed that Mr. " Jack " Wright be elected, and the proposition was seconded by Mr. Smith. The motion WAS carried with applause. —As Mr. Wright has been acting as sub-captain of the team the elec- tion of a successor was necessary. Mr. Houghton sub- mitted the name of Mr. Richaid Johnson, who was sPconded by Mr. H. Binghatn. It so the second team might —(a. voice: " Win it," and cheers)—rnigh: enter and so fill up the vacant dates.—in declaring the business of the meet- ing at an end the Chairman expressed the hope that the members would all try ti make the Fee:roe of the club a successful one. They were rather unfortunate last year, but he hoped that during the coming season they would have Letter performances, and that this time they would have the pleasure bringing the cup to Widnes.—A vote of thanks to the chairman. concluded the proceedings.—lt may be stared that the officers of the club are the hon. sec, 'Mr. John A. Brown ; captain let team; Mr. W. Kiddie; ditto 2nd team, Mr. H. Stirrup ; sub•ceptains Ist team anti 2nd team, Messrs. J li. Selith and J. Wiight ; hon. treasurer, Mr. J. Ashel ; ,ssistant sec., Mr. F. Wright. - dreeesing-room is at the Central Hotel, near the two stations.
LONDON LETIEIL

LONDON, THURSDAY. The session is at last over, and the Ministry are at ease. For at least four months they will be their own masters, undisturbed .by inconvenient ques- tioners. They may involve the country in war, or may take a step similar to that of the`joint occupa- tion of Egypt, which has brought in its train such incalculable disaster; or they may set themselves honestly and heartily to work upon home legisla- tion. 1 believe that if Lord Randolph has his way, and circumstances do not baffle his efforts, that the latter course will be adopted. Constitutionally there is no more rabid reformer in the House ai Commons than the Tory Chancellor of the Ex- chequer. Like his prototype, Mr. Disraeli, he is a Conservative by accident, a Radical by conviction. It is he who is directly responsible for the long pro- cession of Commissions, the appointment of which have marked these earlier days of the Ministry. A policy of Commissions is,. regarded as a matter of ,tactics, an admirable one. (From any point of view it is better than a policy of Mr. Smith.) Whilst the Commissions are inquiring the Government is comfortably seated in office without being ham- pered by any responsibilities. Perhaps they may lig turned out before the Commissions report. If they are not they have gained so much time, and have also in hand more or less valuable material upon which to base legislation. If nothing worse comes of a Conservative Government than the natural issue of the Commissions that have been appointed, the nation will have reason to be thankful. The debate on Mr. Parnell's Bill did not, soar to the fullest height of Parliamentary discussion. It was, from the first, a foregone conclusion. Curiosity was satisfied when it was known what Mr. Glad- stone would do, and what position the Disientient Liberals would take up. These matters ascertained, all traces of interest disappeared, and members waited only for the division. Tkis was aken in a Heuse unprecedently full for the third week in September. The Conservatives had issued an impera- tive Whip, and their mencame up from all corners of the earth. The Parnellites also were sternly brought up to Westminster, and Many faces not familiar to the House appeared in that quarter. Of the 84 members no less than 81 appeared, a fact which speaks volumes for the discipline of the party. 0.2 the Liberals under Mr.`Gladstone:s leadership, who are reckoned at 192, 168 either voted or paired for the bill, leaving only 24 unaccounted for. This is a remarkable demonstration of Liberal feeling, and means a great deal for the future. The Dissentient Liberals were broken up in various ways. Only 31 out of their muster of 76 voted against the bill, two voted for it, and the rest abstained. The absten- tions were, on the whole, perhaps the most remark- able feature of the case, among them being the Chamberlain family, Sir Henry James, Mr. Bright, Mr. Caine, and, Mr. Collings. As to the future, it is regarded with grave mis- givings by the best authorities on Ireland. What the Government think of it is indicated by Sir M. Hicks-Beach's ominons threat that Parliament may be called together before the usual time in order to consider a Coercion Bill. Among the Liberals the hope is that Mr. Parnell and his friends will use their influence to maintain order in the dark times which are close upon us. That eviction will follow is beyond doubt. The Irish toree,is well organised, and of its recources and deterraination we know too much. To submit now, accept the decree of the Conservative majority in the House of Commons, and pay the full rent would be to acknowledge de- feat and- admit the vulnerableness of the Land League. That—will not be allowed. The tenants will refuse to pay more than was offered by Mr. Parnell's Bill, there will be a grievous series of evictions, which the Executive will be bound to see carried out, and then dark days and nights for Ire- land.

I hear of many members of the Liberal side of the House of COMMONS who are giving proof of their inter- est in Ireland in apraetical manner. They are taking their holiday there, which means a great deal more than the expenditure of so many AO notes. A man's interest in a place is certain to be quickened by his personal acquaintance with it, and menibers coming in contact with the kindly nation on the other side of the channel will return to Westmins- ter with fuller determination to do them justice. It will be arciembered that in other times, that seem separated from us by a generation, Mr. Cham- berlain 'conceived this same notion of testifying to his interest in Ireland. lie and Sir Charles Dille were to lave visited the country un search of mate- rial strengthening their hands in bringing forward a scheme for establishing Home Rule in Ireland. But a:great deal has happened since then to both these.itate.smen. Chambeilain has nowsse. t off for hi.s, holiday, au enterprise in which he has ever combined search of information. with the acquire- men. tc)f recreation. But now it is distant Bulgaria wineh claims his sympathies,,a.nd Ireland is left to lamentih is desertion. ,Next.atumn, if 'nothing particular happens in t.he/political horizon, we shall see a new departure ein Parliamentary holiday arrangements. The colonists who have been over here during the season have been Mostperiistent in theirinvitation tomembers whom they have met to make a return vigt. Mr. Henniker Heaton, the member for Can- terbury, himself an Australian, has taken the matter cup, and will next .year organise a party of I.P.'s Who, " pers9aally conducted," shall visit Australia. I know several members, lured by the prospect of -the triumphal preg-ress that awaits them, mean to go. This is*, very desirable development of holiday 'enterprise. Lord Rosebery, who frequently says -Wise things, declared the other day that no one ssk.ould be a Minister of State who has net personally wished the dependencies off the Empire. Lord Rose- 'bury himself hasacted up to this prindple. Three _wears ago he visited Australia, and this autumn he iis bound for India. The advantages Of travel have !been recorded as 'far ha& as the time of Bacon, and ilt is one of the best signs about our recent legisla- tures that members have been keen to visit foreign -countries, and above all oar colonies. It would not e at all a bad thing if it were part of the statutory , duty of a member of Parliament to spend the recess in visiting India and-the colonies: The "World," of Tuesday, repeats in vaguer form ttbe particulars of the, coming Colin Campbell suit, 'which were fully given in this column a fortnight -ago. On a former occasion when this distinguished person appeared in the 'Divorce Court influence from thigh quarters was brought to bear to have the case 'tried in camera. It was felt to be an awkward thing that one connected by family ties with the highest family in the land should have his domestic story told in the public ear. The interference with the ordinary course of judicial procedure proved to be &lamentable failure. The :only result was that the story got into circulation in distorted form, and the 'end was much worse than 'if the ordinary habitude , of the Court had been followed. There will be no further attempt in this direction. The case will be heard in open Court, and the dullness of November will be made deeper 'by the recital, of one of the most miserable stories ever heard, even in the Court over which Sir James Hannen presides. Mr.. Lionel Brough has been forestalling his bio- grapher by giving some accounts of himself to an active interviewer. There must have been a , tinge of sadness in his communications with respect I to the` Daily Telegraph;" for he is able to say that at one time he might have bought two-thirds of that newspaper for the sum of six shillings. Brough, who began life as an office boy in the " Illustrated • London sews," went on to the " Telegraph " in its earliest and' most. impecunious days, when it was in the hands of Colonel Sleigh. AcNmling to Mr. Brough's account, Sleigh introduced two other . gentlemen, a Major Peering and Captain I' put down :2500 each, upon the assurance that there was a proprietary of eight gentlemen who had each . subscribed a similar sum. Some time after, when

(the two proprietors found that this was a mistake, they facetiously offered Brough to sell their shares at three shillings each. He being young and of careful habits, reflected that possession of the paper involved a certain amount of responsibility. His estate might be seized upon to make up deficiencies, and he accordingly declined to entertain the offer. Colonel Sleigh was at the time in debt to the vener- able head of the family which is now sole proprietor of the "Telegraph." Jonas Levy, according to a narrator more familiar than these addenda of Lionel Brough's, bought the paper from Colonel Sleigh for a mere sing. It would take a good many songs, supposing they were currency, to buy the paper . now.

The proposal put forward by the Prince of Wales • for the establishment of a ColOnial Institute in commemoration of the jubilee year has at the out- set been received with the approval that might be expected from a. loyal nation. But there lurks behind the proposal several questions which are likely to develope some unpleasantness. There is a belief in some well-informed quarters that the Prince of Wales is ,made use of by an eminent clique to further their private ends. The new in- stitute, if it be carried out upon the lines roughly sketched in the Prince's letter to the• Lord Mayor, will be managed by a very close corporation. The people are to rind the money, and a select company nominated by the Prince of Wales are to manage the concern. It has very much come to this in the matter of the big exhibition at South Kensington. A peculiar feature in this enterprise is, that whilst its apparent success has been enormous, and its ad- vantages -peculiar, nothing has been heard of a sur- plus nor has any balance sheet been published. That is, at least, not business-like, and if the proposed new scheme is to be broad based upon popular sup- port, it will be necessary that undertaking shall be given that its direction will be placed in other hands.

Ireland, I hear, is starting a new crop this year. Her farmers are seeking to find a source of revenue oat of what most farmers regard as a source of loss. There is a common saying amongst countrymen that three rabbits eat as much as a sheep. This testi- mony to the rabbit's voracity is probably exag- gerated. Certainly in some districts of Ireland the fur is quite plentiful enough to keep down the wool, and rabbits have to be destroyed in the interests of the larger nibbler. But the question is now whether , more might not be done in the same direction on more lucrative terms. The trade with Liverpool and London has been recently developed. It has long existed, but the consignments were only occa- sional. This autumn for the first time it has taken considerable proportions. In these days it is almost as hopeless to think of inventing a new • trade as inventing a new animal. The rabbit as a lucrative export seems likely to solve both difficulties-for the Irish.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of this Bard was held on Thursday afternoon, at the Board-room, Victoria-road, Widnes. Mr. T. S. Timmie presided, and there were also present. Dr. O'Keefe, the Rev. F.ther Finegan, Messrs. Pra Ishaw, D03C013, Robinson, Glover, and Danby (c 1,11

div.head: DIST,ICT IMUCATION commtrrEs.
div.p: DIST,ICT IMUCATION commtrrEs.

Tnia c uninittee rep.irted that during the month of August the numbere of cases summoned before the com- mines were as follows :—Applictrion for pavniefit of fees, 105 ; for csntravention of the F.ducation Act, 243 ; total, 349. Fees were recommended to be paid in 96 cases ; re- fused, 9 ; numb-r of prosecutions before the ma-Es!rates, 42 ; number of convictions, 40 ; sent to Industrial%chools,2.— Mr. Gaskell proposed the adoption of the minutes.—Father Finegan asked if the number of those who were summoned for contravention of the Education Act was increasing ? Mr. Deacon said he was not prepared to say that the number was increasing, but he hoped to be able next month to sub- mit a return for the year. He could not at present say how the number would compare with the previous year, but he ationld imagine that it would be abo4 the same.—Father Finegan said he thought that there were more children from school than there used to be. At his school the teachers complained.—Mr. Deacon said he thought that there had been no falling off in the attendances during the year. .Personally he was rather astonished to find that the figures were so good.—Father Finegan said that he was afraid that tbe outskirts were being neglected, and that the children there were not looked after like they were in the thick of the town.—After a little further discussion the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: RESIGNATION OP A SCHOOLMISTRESS:.
div.p: RESIGNATION OP A SCHOOLMISTRESS:.
The Board accepted the resignation of Miss Longshow, assistant mistress in the infant department of the Simm's Cross school, the engagement to terminate on September 30th, 1886.

div.head: TRH VACANT READ MASTERSHIP.
div.p: TRH VACANT READ MASTERSHIP.

The minutes of the School Manangement Committee contained the following recommendation That Mr. Robert Devonald be appointed head master of the senior boys' department of the Warrington-road schools (vice Mr. Hunter), at a salary of £llB per annum, rising according to the scale of the Board,"and with the additional payments, if earned, as detailed in resolution of the Board No. 1,061; the engagement to date from October Ist, 1886, and to be determinable ore either side by three months' notice, to expire on the last day of any calendar month."— Father Finegan, who proposed the adoption of the minutes, said that there had been about a hundred applications for the post, but Mr. Devonald was well qualified for it,, and the committee gave him the preference, as he was already in the service of the Board. He was certainly rather young, but that was a fault that would right itself. It bad been the custom in the past to give preference to those in their empioy.—The recommendation was adopted.

div.head: NEW CONTRACT.
div.p: NEW CONTRACT.

It was resolved, on the recommendation of the School Management Committee, that the tender of Messrs. Phillip, Son and Nephew be accepted for stationery, exercise -books, drawing books, slates, maps, diagrams, school furniture and apparatus, and kindergarten materials, at the prices named in their schedule (in the place of Messrs. M. A. Thompson and Co . bankrupt). The contract to be in force 'until March 31st, 1887.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The School Management Committee reported as follows: —(a) That they had engaged a teacher on supply to assist Mr. Devonald at the Warrington-read Schotis, from /Ingest 17th until October let, 1886, at a salary of LI 5s per week. (b) That on the application of the Widnes Local Beard, they had released Miss Mullen, teacher of.cookery, from her duties, for three or four days in the last week of September, to give lectures on cookery, in connection with an ekhibi- tion of ga* stoves proposed to be held in the Lacey-street Schootroom.—Approved.

div.head: AVLEGIED SEVERE CORRALVIVNISHMENT.
div.p: AVLEGIED SEVERE CORRALVIVNISHMENT.

Fattier Finegan referred to an 'ltem in the report'of the School Management Committee, which said that 'a severe case of corporal punishment had taken place in the senior boys' department of 'the 'West Bank !Schools. The committee felt, be said, that it was a case that should I not lise passed over without comment. They had within the pest few months issued very strong instruction to the teachers to keep to the rules, -but on more 'than one occasion they had found that the .rules had ntk. been oh- serded. This was one of the occasions, as the rules provi- ded that any case of punishment-should lan reported on a skeet supplied for the purpose, and submitted to the com- mittee. That had not been done.—ln answer to the chair- man, 'Father Finegan said Mr. Bnoddy was theiteacher re- ferred to.—The Chairmasr. Is it'inthe instructions that cot, pozal punishment only be inflicted by the headmaster ? Father Finegan: Yes, and it should be placed en the punish- ment sheet: —After some discussion it was resolved : "The 1 School Management Committee reported titat Thomas Hughes was severely caned on August 11th, and resolved that Mr. Suoddy's attention be called to the rules of the 'Board, and that he be informed that violatioa of those rules ‘may lead>te instant dismissal."

div.head: WARRINGION FARMERS' CLUB
div.p: WARRINGION FARMERS' CLUB
A committee meeting of this club was held on Wednesday evening at the White Bull Inn, Horse- market-street, when the chair was occupied by Mr. John Marsh.
THE DEPRESSION IN AGRICULTURE.

Referring to one of the subjects on the agenda paper Mr. W. DARBYSIIIRE said that he considend that the lowness of the prices now obtained for farm stock and produce was of great importance to all people engaged in agricultural pursuits. Certain sorts of produce were never at lower prices than now. A short time ago .they had many of the lead- . ing men of the country directing the attention of the farmers to the desirability of turning their at- tention to the cultivation of fruit. They had adopted this course during the year, and what was the result? That some kinds of fruit were so plen- tiful that it was scarcely worth while taking it to market, as prices were so low. He next referred to a statement that in Chester market good magnum bonum potatoes were quoted at whole- sale prices as low as .E 2 per ton, or a trifle over.4f lbs for a penny. Under these circumstances, he asked, what profit was left for the farmer ? Mr. JOHN DA.RBYSHIRE said that it was time that they were up and doing, and began to demand con- cessions with regard to tithes. This they were per- fectly justified in doing. There was a gentleman in that room who paid from £3O to £35 a year in tithes, and received no benefit whatever. Farmers had been written down sand talked down, but he would like to ask the newspaper proprietor, repor- ter, land agent, or landlord, if there was any justice in this? Were not commonsense farmers to have a voice in the management of their own affairs? They must be up and doing, and let the country know what they wanted. If they were content to re- main at home and count the cinders, in- stead of telling what their burdens were, those burdens would long remain. (Hear. hear.)— After a little fluffier discussion the SECRETARY (Mr. J. L. Stelfox) read a copy of a manifesto, which it was proposed should be issued by the club. It was resolved that it be issued on the motion of Mr. KNOWLES, geconded by Mr. W. DA.RBYSHIRB. The manifesto points out the advantages which might be derived by all farmers from such institutions as the Warrington Farmers' Club, if they were gener- ously supported. What they wished was to make agriculture profitable—firstly, by decreasing the cost of production; and secondly, by obtaining better prices for farm stock and produce. The ac- lion taken by the club as to the first matter last year had resulted in the remission of rents amount- ing to many thousands of pounds. These remissions were altogether inconsiderable compared with what the justice of the case demanded, and with what would he obtained if farmers presented a firm and united front.

div.head: RENT QUESTION.
div.p: THE RENT QUESTION.

Mr. Taomis STELFOX proposed that a circular be agaid sent to landlords in the district of the cub, asking for a further reduction of rent. The one, they sent out last year, he said, had, directly or in- directly, resulted in the reduction of rents to a large - I amount, and Its the reasons that made them then ask 'for a reduction had now grown still more he thought that another and similar appli- - cation might be made. Potatoes were now at so • low a figure that they were scarcely worth taking to the market. Oats were at threepence and four- - pence per bushel less than last year. Landowners advised them some time ago to give up growing wheat, and now they had taken to oats the price of them was so low as to be unprofitable. The farmer was justified in expecting sufficient to keep him and his family in a respectable position, after he had paid his rates, and the landlord was entitled to a, fair amount of rent, but that must be regulated what.there was left after the things enumerated" had been paid. They had a reduction of 10 per cent 'last year, and he thought they were now entitled to one of 30 per cent.—Mr. JOHN DA_RRYSHIRE thought that it was better that. a memorial should 'issue from the club than that individual farmers• should ask reductions from their landlords.—The resolution was carried. _ THE WELSH FARMERS AND IHi TITHE.

Mr. W. DARBYSIIIRE suggested that the general. meeting of the club be recommended to send a letter. to farmers in Wales, who are struggling against the tithe charge. The letter, he said, might state that the club was alive to the importance of the abolition of tithes, and sympathised with the Welsh in their agitation.—Mr. WRIGHT: It would be rather a good move to say that we approve of the total abolition of rents. (Laughter.)—The SECRETARY said the outrages that had occurred in connection with the tithe agitation in Wales were not the fault of the farmers. The greatest obstruction had been caused by the popular feeling that had been roused among other than farmers. He thought, referring to the remark of Mr. Wright, that in time the tent on agricultural land would be altogether abolished. God gave the land to man, and it should be his.— Mr. WRIGHT argued i that as money had been ex- pended on the land, t was fair that a rent should be ' charged.—The CHAIRMAN said that the present de- pression arose from the foreigner being able to send produce to England without having to pay rates 1 and taxes. Landlords, if they' redeemed tithes, would put something extra on the rents.— After further discussion, it was resolved : "That the members of the Warrington Farmers' Club express their sympathy with the Welsh far- mers in their agitation against the continued pay- ment of that special class-tax, tithes, which, owing to the disappearance of farm profits;has now to be paid out of farm capital, and hope that they will not cease their efforts until the imposition has been fully removed." .It was also resolved that a memo- rial should be sent to the tithe owners in the district 'asking them for a reduction in the amount payable. —This was all the business.
