THE STATE OF IRELAND. On Saturday. night an encounter took place between the police and some Skibbereen fisherman at Youghal, who were being ejected from a public-house. The police drew their swords on the way to the barrack, and one fisherman was seriously injured. On Saturday, the house of a labourer named Daffy, of Drumheriff, near Castlehlaeney, was broken into and the furniture smashed. Duffy is stated to have worked for a boycotted farmer, and to have refused to join the local branch of the National League. On Sunday night, three moonlighters who intended per- petrating an outrage upon a farmer named Brennan, living at Craigbrien, near Ennis, wets surprised by a police pat- rol. Tne moonlighters, who were armed, were called upon to surrender. They ran away, and the police fired after them, but whether the shots took effect is unknown. A Downpatrick correspondent writes that no doubt now exists that a dreadful murder has been committed at B illy- kine, near Ballynahinch, the hady of David Hall, the missing man, having been foaled en Sunday evening in a flaxlaele adjacent to where he was last seen alive. A chain was attached to the body. and large stones were tied to the head and feet. There was a bullet wound on the side of the head. A farmer named Martin, landlord of the house in which the murdered man resided, has been arres- ted on suspicion. THE VICEROY IN DUBLIN.—FATAL RIOTING IN BELFAST. The Marcieis of Londonderry made his State entry into Dublin on Saturday as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland. His Excellency was accompanied from Holyhead in the Royal mail steamer Ireland by the Marchioness of Londonderry and children, the Dowager Marchioness of Londonderry, Captain Swaine, military secretary; and Mr. Mulhall, private secretary. The Ireland steamed into the harbour at a quarter to eight in the morning, and cense alongside the Best Pier. The ships in the harbour were decorated, but there we few persons on the pier. At half-past twelve o'clock a deputation from. the Kingstown Town Commis- sioners went on board, and on the deck of the steamer the Town Clerk read an address welcoming his Excellency to Ireland as her Majesty's representative, and trusting that the wants of Ireland would have his personal study and help. His Excellency, in reply, said he WAS animated by an earnest desire to promote, by all means in his power, the social and material prosperity of "our own native land." At twenty minutes pest twelve the special train started for Westland-row, where it arrived a quarter of an hour later. crowd assembled outside the terminus as the time for the arrival of the train approached, and when his Excellency emerged from the carriage drive on horsebeek a cheer was raised, mingled with some hisses. The procession imme- diately started for the Castle. There was a large crowd in College Green, and as his Excellency passed the Old Par- liament House cheers were called for and given for " Castle- reagh " and the "Union," while there were counter cheers for "Home Rule.' Several pelsons were arrested by the police for disorderly conduct and hooting during the pro- cession. There was a serious renewal of rioting in Belfast on Sun- day night. About half-past seven Patrick Gorman was arrested at the corner of Hammond-street far interfering with a policeman who was endeavouring to prevent a dis- turbance. Constables Allen and Brennan took him ieto custody, and they were both kicked and struck by the prisoner. A crowd collected and shouted that the man had done nothing. The prisoner was conveyed to the Davis- street police barrack, which was immediately surrounded by a mob, who forced down the shutters and threw stones into the barrack, where there were only four constables at the time Constable Dickson went for assistance by the back way to Peter's Hill police barrack, having to scale several walls, and cross a river. In the meantime the police re maining in the barrack fired upon the crowd, and a man named Beyd, 28 years of age, was shot dead. A woman named Kerry was also shot in the head. She died in the Royal Infirmary. A ',ember of others were injured. Four or five policemen were also severely injured. The barrack was partially wrecked before a reinforcement of police arrived. The rioters were charged, and the streets cleared. A detachment of the West Surrey Regiment afterear)s arrived upon the scene. Several arrests were made. There was renewed rioting at Belfast on Monday, arising out of a savage attack made en a number of Queen's Island men when passing through North-street on their way home from the military review in Ormean Park. Showers of mis- sies came from the neighbourhood of Law's court and other alleys running into North-street, and a fierce fusilade was maintained by the opposing crowds, in spite of the efforts of the police to suppress the disturbance. At length a cor- don was drawn aeross the street and the rival mobs kept apart. Two girls, however, were the victims of a brutal as- sault in North-street, and as the police did not attempt to protect them, a Protestant mob on Peter's-hill charged down to their rescue, and fighting recommenced, the stone-throw- ing being continued until large reinforcements of police ar- rived on the scene. Later on, some fighting took place on the worepeople leaving Campbell's large flax spinning mill Fall's-road. The employes, who are both Roman Catholics and Protestants, number several thousand, but there were only five police-officers on duty in the neighbourhood, and they were severely handled on attempting to quell the dis- turbance, the sergeant in charge receiving a dangerous scalp wound. Aid was summoned from Bower's-hill police bar- racks, and a detachment of constabulary was despatched, accompanied by Mr. Lyster, resident magistrate. The mob was charged, but extreme measures were avoided. About five o'clock large crowds assembled in the vicinity of the National League offices, in Fleetwood-street, and attacked those who attempted to enter the premises. There was a good deal of stone throwing, and several arrests were made. With regard to Sunday night's riots, there is feeling amongst the Nationalists that the action of the police in firing on the mob was unjustifiable. At Belfast, on Monday, Patrick Gorman was charged with participating in Sunday night's disturbance, in which two persons wets shot dead by the police. The accused, it was stated, was encouraging two men to fight when he was arrested, and the constables who took him were kicked by several other persons. TheZmob stoned the barracks, and the police fired upon them, with the fatal results stated. The Case was remanded.—Felix Connolly WAS charged with a similar offence. Prisoner demanded at the barracks, the name and number of the constable who ar- rested prisoner Gorman, and on being refused them he attacked the constable, and the .crowd at the same time en- tered and attempted to seise the riles on the rack. Prisoner was committed for trial, bail being accepted.— Thomas Griffiths was sentenced to three months' imprisonment for carrying firearms without a license. He was arrested Cu Sunday night with a revolver in his pocket, loaded in all its six chambers.

div.head: -FIGHTING IN BELFAST.
div.p: -FIGHTING IN BELFAST.

- For a great part of Monday night Millfield was the scene of frequent charges by the police and military, a free use of revolvers being made. A very serious attack was made in Dover-street Brickfields by the Falls-road mob on the Dragoane. One horse reared and the rider was thrown to the ground. At Albert-crescent Barracks the Dragoons charged the mob amid a shower of missiles. In this dis- trict the representatives of the opposing parties met, and the danger of a riot was imminent, but in Shankhill-road the police who sought shelter fro,n the Falls-road mob were protected by the inhabitants. At eleven o'clock the pri- soners who had been taken to Queen-street Barracks were brought to the police office under military escort. The inquest on the bodies of Thomas Boyle and Catherine Kelly was held on Monday evening. The jury returned a verdict ie both cases to the effect that they came to their death from the effect of shots fired by the pollee from Davis-street Barracks. The jury strongly complained that the whole of the constables in the barracks at the time were not forthcoming to give evidence. Sergeant Whelan, who was in command, declined, at his discretion, to give evidence. About nine o'clock on Tuesday morning as 10 work- men were leaving the Clonard Mills on the Falls-road, Bel- fast, a disturbance took place among them, and two sections stoned each other. They then drove a picket of policemen standing at the corner down Albert-street, through the Pound, into Durham-street. District. inspector Ewart arrived with a reinforcement of police and dispersed the mob. With the exception of a slight disturbance as the workmen were leaving their employment on Wednesday night at Messrs. Fulton's print works, Falls-road, Belfast has been quiet. The men were attacked by a Catholic mob, and they retaliated, but the disturbance was quickly suppressed by the police. A large number of prisoners were dealt with by the magistrates in the Custody Court on Wednesday on charges of riot, and most of them were returned for trial at tee assizes. WARRINGTON V. SALFORD. The cup holders on Saturday last journeyed to Manches- ter, to try conclusions with the Salford team.. Fresh from their victory over the strong lot of Swintonians the previous week, they felt confident that if they did not win, they would at -least make a draw of it. bat in this they were mis- taken, as the wearers of the "red" proved one too many, scoring 3 tries and 5 minors to Warrington aikrninorts. The game was far from being so one-sided as the score implies, as the visitors several times had hard lines in not scoring, the chief being, when a rush was made up the field, Rigby taking a prominent part, supported by Gilbert, the ball going over the line, hat owing to a collision between the former and a Sa.ford player, Gilbert WAS prevented from scoring between the posts. On another oceanic)* Ashton picked smartly up, being only brought down within a yard of the goal line. The weather was beautifully fine, and no doubt, owing to this and the prestige of the cap holders, this was the cause of seeing some 3,000 • persons round the enclosure, who were amply repaid by witnessing a very flue , exhibition of football. Salford won the toss, and Frank Turner kicked off with the sun shining in the eves of the visitors. The Warring- ton forwards followed well up, and collared the ball in the home quarters, its stay there being of thort duration, as the ball became loose and was soon taken up the ground. The visitors' forwards, after the first scrimmage, settled down to their work. On a seriminage being formed Ottiwell game through, but Graham relieved to touch. Again the same player came through, only to be stopped by Ashton. The Warrington forwards now, by sheer hard work, took the ball to the home quarters; but some smart play by Williams and Roberts took it back again. Again the Warringtonians worked the ball to half-way, and by another strenuous effort to the home 25, where Graham obtained possession and kicked, the ball going over the line, thus giving Warrington the first minor. From the first scrimmage affer the drop out the home team came through, but Barnes relieved to touch, Slater replying by a nice run and kick to touch. Some severe scaimmages were next the order of the day, until E. Dillon broke away with the ball at his toesonly to be stopped by the Salford Buxton. Gilbert now pseeid to Barnes, who got in a nice run, afterwards kicking to touch in the home 25 ; but Slater, aided by the home forwards, took the leather into the visitors' territory. For some time play was very exciting. Warrington having slightly the ad- vantage in the pack; but Varley kicked wide, the ball falling into the hands of Slater, who evaded Buxton and ran in to the great delight of the spectators, planting the ball be- hind the posts. Rigby charged Varley's kick down, and from tbe kick out Ottiwell and Roberts showed up-promin- ently ; but Fair Turner stepped their progress. Eventually Ottiwell came through and gained ground. Speakman now passed to Graham, who failed to take it. and the "Reds" taking advantage of the mistake quickly took- the ball to the visitors' 25. The visitors' forwards by adetermined rush took the ball to half-wav, and Fair Turner coming up obtained possession, punted, and he and Ashton following up, the ball was forced over the line, a minor resulting. Ottiwell kicked out, Barnes returning to touch. A piece of fine play was next witnessed on the part of Turner, Jolley, and Barnes, who took the ball to the line, but the full back nicely saved. Half time was now called with the hall in the home 25, the score being one try and two minors to two minors for the cupholders. The second half was only a re- petition of the first, being of a much faster character than on the previous week. Another try was obtained for Sal- ford in this half by Williams rushing the ball up the field and getting over the line, Smith falling on it and claiming the try. Slater made a bold bid for goal, but was unsuc- cessful. Warrington towards the end fell off (contrary to their usual form), but still managed to prevent any further scoring, the game at the close standing Salford two tries five minors. Warrington four minors. The chief features of the game were the good piny of Sal- ford on the loose and the Warringtonians in the pack. The backs had very little to do, the game chiefly being a forward one. Buxton, at back, did net by any means play up to his usual form, as both tries were obtained through misjudg- ing the ball in the first place, and secondly through failing to hold it when in his possession; but in the game of foot- ball the best of players,at times are liable to make mistakes, and this se itned to be one of the little full' back's unlucky days. Barnes was the pick of the three-quarters, doing an immense amount of work in good style. Jolley seems to be getting better in the picking up department, but does not seem to get away so readily; but on Saturday last both he and Graham had very few chances of distinguish- ing themselves. The two half-backs- (who are both on the sick list) played remarkably well, when we consider their case, and pitted as they were against two,of the best half- backs in the county. The forwards, one and all, str ye hard to avert defeat. H Ashton showed up most prominently, being well followed by the brothers- Turner, Povey, Rigby, and Hayes. In the back division of Salford Slater was the best of the trio, kicking and running well. R. Walmsley played a geod game, when it is taken into consideration that this was his first appearance for nearly two years. Clegg was the best of the two halves,.and ,Ottiwell, Roberts, and Williams in the forwards. Teams.—Warrington : Buxton, back; Jolley, Barnes, Graham, three-quarter backs; Gilbert and Speakman, half- backs; Fair. 'I urner, Frank Turner,. Hayes, Rigby, Davies, E. EARLESTOWN V. CREWE ALEXANDRA.—The visit of the Crewe Alexandra first team to Earlestown on Saturday afternoon excited a keen interest in football circles, and the splendid ground of the Earlestown club, the Meanes, was surrounded by a large crowd of interested spectators. The visitors came with a famous reputation., and a decisive de- feat of the home team was generally anticipated. These anticipations proved to be unfounded, however, for the game was one of the hardest and evenly contested matches witnessed on the ground. The Crewe team mustered a strong eleven, while the home team,. re-organised and rear- ranged, was also a very strong ona. Having won the toss the Earlestonians elected to play uphill with a strong wind and a brilliant sun at their backs. For a few minutes the visitors played well, but the Earlestown backs, who played brilliantly throughotat, repulsed all attacks. The home for- wards made some good runs, and after about twenty minutta play. Sims, after a capital pass from the left wing, sent the ball threugh the Crewe uprights amid loud cheers. The visitors made determined attempts to secure an equalising point, and in this they were successful before half time was called. Ends were changed with the score one goal each, and the game was resumed amid increasing ecitement. Directly after the kick off the Crewe forwards rushed in front of the Earlestown goal, and to the surprise of the sup.

porters of the home team, the visitors notched a second goal by a swift shot from the centre. A claim of off-side was made by the home players, but the referee decided in favour of the visitors, who thus took a lead. Not many militates had elapsed before, from a long shot on the tight wing, Champion caught the ball, .but it twisted from his hands and through the goal, an unfortunat mighak which resulted in the defeat of the home t3am.. The Earlestown team again srarted the ball with the score three goals to one against them, and from this point they unmistakeably had the advantage. The foe sad backs and goal keeper were fond plenty ofwork,and they worked bard and well. Ten minutes front the finish a scrimmage in front of the Crewe goal resulted in Siddeley notching a second goal for the home team amid loud cheers. The play of the remaining few minutes was very exciting, bat no further point was scored, and Crewe thus won by three goals to two. The game throughort had been a capi- tal one. Both goal-keepers had some dangerous shots to stop, but the feature of the game was the•splendid play of Captain Green and Clough for Earlestewn. These two were repeatedly cheered for their splendid kicking and tackling. Whalley also played well. Among the forwards the brothers Shaw put in some capital passing, while the runs of Sims and Ellison were at times very fine. The Crewe team played well to a man, but the brilliant runs of E. Payne on the outside right wing were most prominent. The players were as follows :—Earlestown T. Champion, goal R. Green (eaptlin) and G. Clough, backs Bowker, and J. Green, half-backs; J. Ellison, and J. W. Sims, right wing; T. :Sicidelev, centre; J. Shaw and W. Show, left wing. Crire Alexandra: G. Heashall, goal ; C. Conde and G. PiTycherley, backs; A. T. Bell, F. Halfpenny, and A Vickerman, half backs ; J. Pearson, A. Payne, E. Payne, P. Ellis, and G. Priee, lorwards. WIGAN ASSOCIATION CHALLENGE CU?.

INFLUENCE OF OXYGEN ON IRON. The first meeting of the session of the members• of the South Staffordshire Institute of Iron and Steel W. orks Managers was held at Dudley, on Saturday, when Mr. Thomas Morris, F.G.S., of War- rington, read an interesting paper on "The influence of Oxygen on the Iron during the Puddling Process, and its Effect in the Engineering Shop." Mr. Fisher, president of the Institute, was in the chair. Mr. Morris explained that he was induced to study the question of the influence of: oxygen by the breakage, two or three years ago, of a shaft belong- ing to one of thellargest Atlantic liners. When the disabled vessel arrived in port the makers had a bar; cut from the fractured part of the shaft and tested it for torsion. The bar broke before it had gone a quarter round, though the original iron from which the shaft had been made had stood' twisting round six times before fracture. Drillings were taken from both these test bars, and the results of an analytical examination were almost identical. The analyses were as, follow :—Good bar—phosphorus, •22; silicon, .12; sulphur, .01 ; manganese, trace; carbon, trace; iron, 99.65. Bad bar—phosphorus, l 8; silicon, l 5;. sulphur, 01;. managanese, 04;. carbon, bare traoe ; iron, 99.62. When consulted by the analyst Mr. Morris explained.. at once that the weakness originated from the presence of oxgyen which had been absorbed, and which was over and above what they found in combination with phosphoric or silicic acid. This gas, he contended, did its evil work when the iron was in a spongy. state, or, in more familiar language, when iron was ready for balling up. These interviews gave- rise to other questions, and amongst them was the origin of the black streaks and patches which appeared on shaft- ing that had been made from supposed clean puddled iron. His theory was that the air had played upon the • iron while or when the ball was being made, and that the oxide formed was pocketed inside the ball, and was not seen again until the ' iron had been turned with the lathe: After explain- ing the process of puddling, Mr. Morris exhibited two pieces of puddled bar iron. One piece was cut from a bar rolls4d from the first ball that was brought out of the furnace, and the, other from a bar that was rolled from the last bali. On testing the first iron for fibre it gave, for puddled iron and for turning, excellent results. The other, taken from the same heat, was exposed to atmospheric air before being taken from the furnace, and, on being tested, it showed-rubsolutely no capability of twist- ing. Tha difference between tiles& two pieces of iron in strengthand ductility, although taken from the same heat, was immense. The former showed a face on being turned that was clean and bright and pleasant to look upon ; the other, a face scorbutic- looking and repulsive. Other samples demonstrat- ing the truth of-Mr. Morris's theory were shown. These included three pieces cut from the bars that were rolled from the first, last, and fourth balls, five balls being made in the heat. They were two inch by three-quarter inch bars, cut in lengths of about 20in., and heated red hot, and swaged to about lin. diameter. They were afterwards turned and bur- nished, and pulled in a testing machine until they broke. Tll4 fellowing were the tests :

--- - . The tensile, strain borne, the' reduction of area, and elongation given by specimen F were, Mr. Morris observed, simply marvellous, and would not: be expectedlay any one from a puddled bar. Not feeling quite satisfied, he took another piece from the same bar, and had It reduced to kin. in thick- ness with a half-round file, leaving the sides or edges as they left the rolls, and this stood even a: greater strain by over two tons. This he considered all that could be desired from the best of workmen lie hardly thought it would he possible to produce a more perfect result; it had just sufficient, and not a superfluous atom of oxygen. Ile believed that the only oxygen that the iron got was obtained from the silicates during decarbonisation. The iron, from which specimen G was produced, had precisely 'the same treatment up to the time it was ready for balling,,and at this stage the air was allowed to play upon it. The iron being hot and still spongy, it was., literally speaking,. eaten up by oxidation, caused. by the air passing:through the working. hole on to it. The difference inthe behaviour of these-two balls-w-hen being shingled under the hammer was very marked. The first gentle pressure on the ball sample F forced the cinder-out of every pore, leaving the ball with a clean round skin, while the ball sample G was as dry under the hammer as though so: many wood shavings. had been balled up and taken to it. In producing the fourth ball, specimen GI, very:different treatrhent had to be used. Instead of allowing this portion of the iron to. get its equivalent of oxygen, it was-allowed to Irest and be stagnant. Whilst lying so, the oxygen of the silicates could not combine with.. the carbon of this part of the metal, while, at the same time, the other, part of: the heat was being worked properly and coming to perfection. Thus, lying on • the bottom, and not being stirred by, the rabble, it : was raw when it ought to be ripe. It was not his : province in thispaper to dilate upon,the action and the effects of the deleterious substances, phosphorus and sulphur, but he thought that he was right in saying that one. or the other, or both, were found in almost, if not in all, pig iron that -was.made, and up-, to that time no economical method: had been found'.' whereby those- hurtful metalloids. could be got rid, of during the. puddling process,. Supposing such could be done, they would be having the Cleveland iron of Middlesbrough competing with the famous' iron of Earl Dudley or the: hest Yorkshire inns. Adverting to the influence of' oxygen in the turning shop, Mr. Morris said that as a destroyer of tools it had no, parallel. The same. tool that would scarcely finish turning specimen 61-, would finish twenty specimens of quality 10.—In the discussion which followed:, Mr. Tucker denied that the injury to tools- resulted from oxygen. There was no 4,,pparent reason,, he contended, vKliy oxide of iron, which was fairly soft, should become brittle and spoil the edge. 0,2 the tools.—Other members having Spoken' a vote of thanks to Mr. Morris for his 7 paper con- . eluded the proceeangs.-- The Iron and Coal Traded Review.

EARLESTOWN BOWLINO Clan. —The members of this club played a handicap of bowls on Saturday for a priz9, presented by Nr. E. T. Evans. The green being in fit at- class condition, caused great excitement to be shown throughout the game. After a splendid afternoon's play, the game was brought to a close with the following result: —Henry Stanton, first; J. Carney, second, and A. Pimblett, third.

THam).—This match took place at Runcorn on Saturday, when a good game was played, resulting in an easy win for the home team by two goals, three tries, and seven minor points, to Wavertree nil. W. quarterbacks; Whitby and Clare, halt backs; Dunbavand, Stubbs, Poland, P. Riley, T. Cox, Abrawis, Ford, Hancock, and Snowball, forwards. Wavertree—W. Morton, back ; F. Woodward, P. Morton. and W. WIGAi lowr END. This match was played on the ground of the latter OR Saturday. The home I team, winning the toss, elected to play with the wind and hill in their favour. Sankey kicked off and very soon forced a minor. After the drop out fr) me good scrimmages took place on the home goal line. Then the home team broke away and scored a minor. The home team still

pressed and scored another minor. After half-time the home team having kicked off, Sankey immediately regis- tered a minor. After this, Sankey penned the home team to their goal line. -and Barton getting hold from a scrim- mage scored a try, the same player kicking a goal, Sankey still pressed and rushed the ball over the line, Jefferson getting a try and Barton again kicking a goal. The game was very exciting from beginning to the end. The first half three minors only being scored for the home team. The tries were ontained by W. Catterall and J. Whittaker, James Hill and Joseph Pritchard failing to kick goals. W. Wright, E. Lavrlesee and W. Graham played well for the horns team, and the visitors were well represented by A. Whittaker. H. Williams, W. Catterall, J. W. Pritchard, T. Dunboe, F. Cooper, G. Hargraves, J. Jackson, J. Dobson, forwards. Widnes: A. Owen, full back ;S. Runt, P. Umpires: J. Lomax and W. Davies. Referee : John Warburten (Wigan). RUNCORN v. LERIIII PARISH CHURCH.—The Runcorn first team on Saturday travelled to Leeds to meet the Parish Church Recreation Club. Some four or five thousand spectators witnessed the match. The general play was evenly balanced, a hotly-eentested match ending in favour of Runcorn by one goal to Parish Church one try, one touchdown, and two dead balls. The Runcorn forwards did their work well, holding their own in the packs and collar- ing in their Usual style. In the backs Andrews and Woods saved repeatedly when danger was apparent, whilst they were most ably supported by Davies' Lunt. Speakinan, and H Hughes. Northend, the home back, played his part finely, always getting clear of his charge admirably. Of the other backs the Brothers Goldthorp played a good safe game; Odde, Greenwood, and Ellewell being the choice of a smart lot of forwards. The teams were :—Leeds Parish Church : J. Northend, back ; ;. Goldthorp, John Goldthorp, and E. Chew, three-quarter backs; H. B. Hammons and W. I Watson, half backs; U. Greenwood, J. Oddy, R. Lumley, J. I Ellewell, F. Riley. B. Dickeeson, R. Turner, S. Green, and R. Leech, forwards. Runcorn: I'. Woods, back; E. Lunt, T. 1 Davie', and H. C. Speakman, three-quarter backs;. H. Hughes and H. Andrews. half backs; W. Wright, W. ' Hughes, J. Lewis, J. Dean, W. H. Broady, Fe G. Joule, G. Wainwright, J. Clarke, and W. Faulkner, for- wards. ST. HilLifics v. TOTTINGTON.—On Saturday the St. Helens football Cluu commenced its season, when a match was played against the Tottington fifteen. The local team sus- tained a somewhat heavy defeat, but several of the players exhibited excellent form, which gives promise of a success- ful season. Borthwick, the visitors' captain, won the toss, and Worthiugton, the Tottington captain, kicked off. The kick sent the ball over the visitors' line, and a touchdown was iminediately registered. Borthwick dropped out from the 25 yards flag, and the ball being well followed up, several smart scrimmages took place. Worthington got possession of the leather, and dropped a splendid goal. lorthwick re-started, and the ball was taken into the borne team's quarters. From a line out one of the Tottington men got hold and rushed it over the line, and gained a try. Borthwick appealed to the referee, on the ground that the ball had been thrown forward, but the point was allowed. Barton kicked a goal for the place kick, and half time im- mediately followed, Borthwick kicked off, and the St. Helens men worked with a will, and gained a decided ad- vantage, but could not score. After some clever passing by Green and Halton, Foreman made a dashing run across the geld, but fell when near the goal line owing to the rough condition of the ground. Soon after this the home 'team gained a try, which was converted into the major point. After this, Halton made a splendid attempt to score, that was knocked into touch close to the goal line. Some I clever scrimmaging took place in the centre, from which Halton secured and dribbled the ball past all the opposing team, and scored a splendid try, but Borthwick did not im- prove the point. An excellent game cone uded, with the score as follows :—Tottington, three goals and six minor points; St. Helens, one try and eight minors. For the , visitors, Foreman, Halton, and Tickle played an excellent game at three-quarter; whilst Borthwick, Pennington, and Basnett distinguished themselves in the forward section. SALFORD V. WARRINGTON (" A " TEAMS) This match was played at Warrington on Saturday, in the presence of I,4oospectators. The game conainenced by:Butter- worth kicking off for Salford, but owing to an infringement of the off side rule, the ball was called back and a scrim- mage formed at half-way, from which Whittle obtained pos• session, nod passing to Appletor., the latter kicked into touch. From the " line-out " Fletcher secured the ball, and punted well up the field, and Massey, who was the recipient, returned the leather in grand 'style. Some give and take play was indulged in until Jones improved matters by breaking away in a eplendid dribble. The visitors were now very sorely pressed, but commenced to reciprocate the attack, and turned the game for a short time somewhat in their favour, through Hewitt failing to return a punt by Mallinson. Littbswood, however, broke through the scrim• mace with the ball at his feet and relieved his side by tak- ing same to half way. Mallinson, obtaining possession, re- turned the ball, and Unsworth securing same made a capi- tal run of half the length of the field. Massey, from passes ' through the hands of Walsh and Appleton, was enablei to gain a try, which point Walsh failed to improve Nothing noteworthy occurred until the call of half time, with the exception of Hughes and Littlewood repeatedly breaking through the scrimmages. On resuming the game Whittle was the first to be conspicuous by a short dodgey run, and and Appleton next by a drop at goal, but failed to obtain the coveted point. The visitors now made another effort to improve matters, and gradually took the ball to the home , 25, but Nevins, Unsworth, Molyneux, and Walsh home- diatelv rushed it back, and succeeded in crossing the lines, and compelled Peynes to touchdown. ' The ball was no sooner brought out again than the home forwards took it back and again compelled Payne to touch down. Directly after this time was called. leaving Warrington victorious by I try and 3 minors to nil. The result of the game affords a pretty fair index of its character throughout. The War- rington team showed a decided superiority to their oppo- nents, especially in the matter of combination, the Salford men at times playing very loosely. They were, perhape, best in the scrimmages, but even here they were generally outplayed. The fault in the Warrington-play was an appa- rent reluctance to take the full advantage of the passing game, Massey having, in consequence, few opportunities given him of displaying his well-known qualities. On the whole, however, the " A " team made an extremely pro- miming debut for the season.

DESIMTING, A FAMILY—At the Proscot Petty sea" sions on Tuetaav, before Mr. W. Pilkington and Colonel Gamble. John Casey, a labourer, formerly employed at the Globe Alkali Work,, St. Helens, was charged under a war- rant with deserting his wife and two children, leaving therm charzeable to the Preecot Union. Ur. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Board of Guardiaes, prosecuted.—From the evidence it appeared that on, the 28th August, the prisoner's wife applied•to Mr. O. M..Barten, relieving officer, for relief for herself and two children. She then stated that her husband had left her on the 10th or the previous month and she was quite destitute. The prisomer when he left was earning 258 Iper week. He was apprehended at Carrick-on-Fergus, Ire- land, the previous day. For the defence the prisoner stated that he went away to his mother in Ireland because of ill- health, and with the full consent of his wife who was per- fectly well aware as to where he was going. Ile was sent to gaol for a month. RICKLESE,DIIITINCP—On Tneeday, at the Preecot Petty Sessions, before Mr. We Pilkington and Colonel. Gamble, John Blackley,,of Liverpool,. was summoned far driving on the wrong side of the road at Preseot, on the 13th. Septem- ber. Mr. Superintendent Barker said that at half-past seven o'clock on Monday, the 13th lust, he was drivipg from Baiehill to Preecot whex the defendant, who was driving a horse and carriage, drove ur:eand passed him on the wrong side of the road,' position which he kept for some dietante. He remonstrated with the defendant, who commenced to curse and swear at him and'attempted his utmost to inter- lock his carriage-wheel with hie. In order to get out of de- fendant's way he had to drive furionsly. On getting into the police etationehe sent a couple of policemen out to ap- prehend the defendant. Blackley was brought up the fol- lowing morning before Mr. Earle and fined 105 and coats for being drunk.' How the defendant managed to emeal,* without runding over same one he did not know. He will the person who erected the lighthouse at the Liverpool ex- hibition, and waat• in well-to-do circomstances. We had . never seen a more reckless MaR for a long time. The de- fendant did not appear, bet a medical certificate was pat in stating he was too ill to attend the court. The Bench iniiiite- ted a tine of I.'oB and costs. The money was paid.

It may he staled that the erection of an organ gallery for tbe chapel was commenced a lew wee'se -ago' and the greatest part of the cost is expected to be cleared by a heeler on an exarrisive scale to be held early next year. After the pro- ceedings had been commenced with singing and prayer, the Chairman (Rev. J2IIIXS Kent, resident minister) briefly touched upon the objects and aims of the fruit banquet, and its connection with the forhconeing bazaar, He stated the alterations and improvements to the chapel included the erection of an organ gallery and vestries at cost of about £51)0, and the introduction of an organ next year, at a ftirther cost of of about £4OO. Hs commented upon the appropriateness of a fruit banquet, such as that gathering, at the present time, and spoke of the importance of each one sowing good seed in all their acts and dealings. The evening's programme included songs be Dr. Nagai, of Golborne, and Mee Need- ham ; recitations by Miss S. J. Aldersonand Mr. Webster; readings by Mr. G-eorge Burgess and Mr. George Haworth ; vocal duet by Miss Roberts and Mr. Atkinson ' • pianoforte duets by the Misses Greenalleand Williams, and the Misses Edwards and Schumacher and a dialogue by Messrs. Glover and Tuft. An interesting feature of the preceedinge, was the distribution of fruit e which was- greatly enjeyed anti appreciated by all present.

MAJESTY'S JUBILEE. LETTER FROM THE PRINCE OF WALES. The following correspondence is officially pub- lished :---- "Marlborough House, Sept. 13, tBS6.—Dear Lord Mayor,—My attention has been frequently called to the general anxiety that is felt to commemorate in some special manner the approaching jubilee of her Majesty's reign. It appears to me that no more suit- able memorial could be suggested than an in- stute which should represent the arts, manufac- tures, and commerce of the Queen's Colonial and In- dian Empire. Such an institution would, it seems to me, be singularly appropriate to the occasion, for it would illustrate the progress already made during her Majesty's reign in the Colonial and Indian dominions, while it would record year by year the development of the empire in the arts of civiiisation. It would thus be deeply interesting to her Majesty's subjects, both within and beyond these islands, and would tend to t,,imulate emigration to those British territories where it 18 required to expand the trade between the dif- ferent British communities, and to draw closer the bonds which unite the empire, It would be at once a museum, an exhibition, and the proper locality for discussion of Colonial and indien subjects. That public attention has already been forcibly. directed to these questions is sufficiently proved by the remarkEtble success w)sich is attend- ing the Colonial and Indian Exhibition at South Kensington, and I confidently anticipate that arrange- ments may be made whereby the more important col- lections, which have so largely contributed to this success, will be placed at the disposal of the institu- tion. I have much satisfaction in addressing this letter to your lordship as chief magistrate of the capital of the Empire, and to invite your co-operation in the formation of this Imperial Institute of the Colonies and India, as the memorial of her Majesty's jubilee by her subjects. Should your lordship con- cur in this proposal and be willing to open a fund at the M ansion House, I would suegest that the contri- butions received be vested in body of trustees, whom the Sovereign would be asked to nominate; and I would further suggest that the institution should be under the permanent presidency of the Heir Apparent to the Throne.-L--I remain, dear Lord Mayor, yours truly, ALBERT EDWARD, P.T.—The Right Hon. the Lord Mayor." The Lord Mayor's reply is as follows:—" The Mansion House, .bondon, September 17. —Sir,--I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Royal Highness's letter of the 13th inst., and, in re- ply, to express the great pleasure it will afford me to give the heartiest co-operation and aid in the forma- tion of the proposed Imperial Institute of the Colonies and India, as the memorial of her Majesty's jubilee by her subjects. Your Royal Highness truly states that general anxiety is felt to commemorate in some special manner the approaching jubilee of her Majesty's reign. There will, lam sure, be a univer- sal desire to give expression in a suitable, and, if pos- sible, adequate way, to the deep attachment, venera- tion, and loyalty which the Queen's subjects, in all parts of her vast dominion, entertain for a sovereign whose long and illustrious reign has been productive of many blessings to her people, and been rendered memorable by the striking progress in civilisation and prosperity throughout the empire. Difficult as it may be to signalise in a commensurate way the feel- ings which are thus naturally emphasised at the ap- proach of the jubilee of her Majesty's reign, lam convinced that the proposal which your Royal High- ness indicates, and which has the support of your in- fluence, will be considered singularly appropriate. /t will therefore give me much satisfaction to open a fund at the Mansion House for the receipt of contri- butions, as suggested by your Royal Highnese.—l have the honour to remain, sir, with the greatest res- pect, your Royal Highness's most dutiful and most obedient servant, JOHN STAPLES, Lord Mayor.—His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, K.G."

SERIOUS COLLISION BLITWEBN TRAINING SHIPS.—An alarming collision took place in Plymouth Sound on Mon- day morning, the training brig Pilot running into the train- ing brig Nautilus whilst the latter was at anchor between Drake's Island and the main. The ships were cleared in about a quitter of an hour, and it was than found that the starboard quarter of the Nautilus had been carried away and a large hole pierced in the hull. She also sustained other minor damages. The Pilot lost her topgallant mast, jibboom, and other headgear, but no one was injured from the falling wreckage. POISONBRS.—At the Central Crinainal Court on Saturday John Reynolds, 32, barman, was convicted of attempting to murder his wife by administering poison to her. The prisoner, who was passing, as a single man at the tavern where he was employed, had promised marriage to the cook, and the evidence left no doubt that he made a very deliber- ate effort to rid himself of his wife by means of sulphate of copper placed in some refreshments which she had while taking a holiday with him at Southend. Mr. Justice Wills characterised the crime as of the foulest and cruellest kind, and sentenced the prisoner to 20 years' penal servitude.—At Wandsworth, on Saturday, a young woman who had been in service at the residence of Dr. Hayfield, Lavender Hill, was committed for trial charged with attempting to poison Mrs. Darling, mother of Mrs. Hayfield. The girl stated that after quarrelling with a fellow-servant, she poured "something from several bottles in the surgery" into the teapot, and added a quantity of laudanum to the milk. She' thought the blame for " what migitt happen" would fall on the other &smut. Mrs. Darling drank some tea and milk, and beeanse seriously ill. THE " BONA-FIDE " LODGER.

Sir,—lf we are to believe all that is divulged upon oath in the Revision Court what distressing revelations of the inner life of Warrington we have ; and what examples of domegic tyranny and filial ingratitude. Young men wins carry the outward semblance of extreme immaturity, and whose youthful countenances are singularly destitute of any- thing in the nature of hirsute ornamentation come forward and declare that they are entitled to be enrolled in the noble army of "bona-fide lodgers," and to sway the destinies of :their country at the ballot box. When invited to show r. ause why they should have their names inscribed on the magic lists what a tale do they unfold. They live with their parents in a cottage. That is the idyllic beginning, but, unfortunately, the idyll ends at the beginning; the love and setf-abnegation which the poetically-minded always asso- ciate with " life in a cottage " form no part of the creed of your " bona-fide ledger." The cottage, the story proceeds, is small it contains only three, four, or perhaps five rooms. Two of these rooms are invariably larger, better furnished. and in every way more comfortable than the others, and thes: are the two that the" boos-tide" always claims as his own. He is but one member of a family which comprises father and mother and, it may be, the full number of other olive branches, besides himself, which people who live in cottages are liable to indulge in, but the two best noms are consecrated to his exclusive use. All the other members of the family are jealously shut out, except upon an odd occa- sion, when, having listened to their humble supplication, be graciously permits them to enter in far a brief season. Ile is in short a veritable little Coeser. He bestrides the domestic establishment like a colossus, and the rest of the inmates have to peep round to find an obscure corner in -which to hide their insignificance. As I said at the beginning, what distressing revelations of the inner life of Warrington are these I To relieve one's feelings one is almost driven to hope that the " bona-fide " young man is not quite so im- portant a personage at home as he would have it believed at the Revision Court. JAGO. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—WORKMEN'S SHARES.

Sir,—The consolidation of the goodwill and energy of the friends of the Manchester Ship Canal is the object of many recent writers in the newspapers who have advocated various metLods of enabling working men to become partners in the enterprise. That there are many thousands of working men in this district who have examined the merits and who have faith in the commercie, eoundnese of the undertaking no one will deny, and if meee elle be devised to enable these to assist eath according to Ite. ability, there will be an economy and utilisation of f-re_ erthy of the reputation of the men of the ccuntv of L.:7“: .'er, famous for its records of individual self-help..but still elore famous as the shire in which that difficult eocial problem, the fusion of capital and labour, •iret found a happy solution, of which we have abundant evidence in those triumphs of comradeship, the active works. mills, warehouses, and fleet of fine steamships busily and profitably employed, belonging to the various wealthy Co-operative Societies. The discussion of the different plans to enable workmen to assist at the present moment is particularly interesting, for the new prospectus of the company will soon be published. There are, therefore, many obvious urgent reasons why all who have thought at all on the subject should assist to de- vise and mature shareholding facilities for those who exist in the greatest numbers in this district, and who might, if they are wise, to be most concerned, and to take the deepest interest in the success of the undertakirg. Permit me to say that this letter iS entirely unofficial. I alone am responsible for its contents, and if the scheme which I propose does not command support by its simplicity let it sink into oblivion. That the money will be obtained I have not the slightest doubt. A working-man told me the other day, "It will be found if the directors give people more time than it takes an egg to boil to subscribe the capital." All schemes proposed to enable working-men to assist the Manchester Ship Canal should have for their object the subscription of the requisite amount of capital within the time required by Parliament before the work can be permit- ted to proceed, and any method which is weak in this direc- tion may be considered comparatively useless for promoting the chief end in view.

All who discuss this question must keep this distinctly in their minds, which I will reiterate in another form—that each and all intending shareholders must have their names registered its the books of the company as quickly as pee- sible after the flew prospectus is issued, for although there may be many thousand men who may be subecribing small sums which would ultimately entitle them to be share- holders, such names will be of little value unless they in- fluence the total amonet required to maintain the legal position of the company, which must have in its records the names of shareholders responsible for five million pounds sterling (exclusive of the purchase money of the Brid,eewater Canal) before the works can proceed, and this must be done before the middle of next year. The sum required to enable a shareholder's name to be entered in the books of the company is £l, and this I would propose to be the sum paid on application for a workman's share. A pound may be considered a comparatively brae sum, and so it is to working-men. but if a man pave £1 down be will take some troehle to protect that pound by paying the remainder of the £lO share. This I propose should be paid at the rate of is a week, so that in 31 years, or about 180 weeks, the £lO share would be paid up. In- terest wculd, of course, be added at the end of every finan- cial year, co that if the amount paid by instalments 'f.f ert. slightly in advance of that of the ordinary shareholders. a portion of the share would be treated as " paid up,'' and re- ceive interest accordingly. The method of collecting these small subscriptions would be very simple. The shareholder having paid his £1 would be provided with a book containing the allotment certificate. The book would consist of half a dozen pages, having spaces for 180 ship canal adhesive stem° coupons. Each stamp would have on its face a consecutive number, and v,hen placed in position would have on it also the initials of the collector or agent When paid up the book could be ex- changed for the £l.O share certificate of the company. The book might be a negotiable instrument by payment of a small registration fee at the offices of the company when sold by the owner.

Agents would be appointed to canvass for and obtain ilhareholders, and to call for the shillings each week. Thess agents would receive a commission equal to that which is sow paid for similar work, and equal to that paid for col- lecting cottage rents. These shillings could be cr.:lkctod without nelnch trouble, and on this point I may say that I have had the bent-fit of the advice of a great number of rent collectw, cf agents a sick and benefit sc,cieties, and c.f periodicalg by weekly payments; indeed, agents who sell those woo know anything at all about the working of mutual aid societies of this connt'y will be aware that there need Le no difficulty in connection with this perti,ln of the schLrm,. div.head: PROPOSED LIBERAL CLUB FOR!
div.p: THE PROPOSED LIBERAL CLUB FOR!
RUAORN.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of Liberals was held in Bethesda Schoolroom, Runcorn, in further- ance of the movement to establish a Liberal club for Runcorn. Mr. B. Kniveton occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. W. Hand- ley, T. Clegg (secretary), S. C. Beckett, J. 'W ill ett , J. Clarke, Sze. The Chairman stated that at a meeting held a few days previously a sub-committee was appointed to draw up rules, to be submitted to a larger meeting. The rules had been drawn up, and would now be submitted. The Secretary then read the rules. It was proposed to call the club the Runcorn Liberal Club, and its objects would be to diffuse Liberal views on political subjects, to pro- mote and secure reform in Parliamentary and other matters, to strengthen and extend unity amongst the Liberals of the town, and to attend to the regis- ter of voters. Each rule was put to the meeting separately and adopted, and it was resolved that the age of membership be eighteen years and up- wards, and that the subscription be 6s. per annum, paid quarterly in advance.

div.head: AN UN HAPPY MARRIAGE.
div.p: AN UN HAPPY MARRIAGE.
SERIOUS ALLEGATIONS.

At the Warrington Borough Court, yesterday, a young man named John Coyne, who resides with his parents in Lincoln-street, was summoned by his wife, Jane Coyne, who charged him with assaulting her on the 18th of the present month. Mr. P. Da- vies appeared for the defence. The parties con- cerned had been married about three years, and the complainant attended court with an infant in her arms. Her story was to the effect that on the morning of the day in question, she went to the house of the defendant's mother, where she saw her husband, and asked him for the baby, which was in his charge. He said that it was not her baby, but his, and his mother said that witness was bad, and that her two children were Ina. Defendant ordered her out of the house, and she said that she would not go without the baby. He then tried to push her out, threw her on the sofa, and caught hold of her by the throat. That was the assault complained of. Asked if she had any witnesses to bear out her statement, complainant replied that she had not sufficient money with which to issue summonses to compel witnesses to attend conse- quently she had not any present. Mr. Davies then said he had a perfect answer to the case. He ac- cused Mrs. Coyne of being of drunken habits, and of getting her husband into debt. He also said that the complainant had niade an attempt to drown herself and her child in a brick pit. Mr. Davies (to complainant) : Did you go to the brick fields with your child ? Yes, but I had no intention.—Mr. Davies: Did you take your child in your arms, and throw it into the pit? No, sir.—Did you intend to do it? No, sir.—Did he run up to you and pull you away from. the pit? No, sir.—Were you not very drunk and excited? I was not. I had only a little money to draw from the mill.—Had you not been in a public- house that day? No, sir.—Were you not threaten- ing to drown yourself and your baby? I was not going to drown my baby.—Did not you say you would do? He told me to drown myself, and I said , I would do so.—Did you not jump into the brick pit? I ran through it.—Who pulled you out of the brick pit? Two young fellows.—Did not your hus- band, after you were pulled out of the pit come to you and hold you, and send for the police? No, he took me to his mother's home.—Did not the police come up ? • Yes, sir.—No further evidence was called, and the Bench discharged the defendant, who received a good character from his employers.

There was a good attendance at both the afternoon and evening ser- vices. Collections were made at the close of each service in aid of the chapel trust fund. WESLEYAN HARVEST THANZSOIVING.—On Sunday har- vest thanksgiving services were held in the Wesleyan Chapel, Rushgreen. At each service the sermon was preached by the Rev. M. Riggall, of Diclsbury, late of War- rington. The chapel was beautifully decorated with fruit and flowers, and there was a large con2regation at each ser- vice. The collections are to be devoted to circuit and local expenses.

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT APSOCIATION.—On Monday, even- ing a meeting of the members of the above association was held in the Wesl..yan Chapel, Lvmm. Mr. John Newburn presided. The Rev G W Guest was the officiating clergyman, the service being choral. As the Party left the church Dr Fox played Men- delssohn's Wedaing march." The bridesmaids were Miss Amy Clegg, Miss Edith Clegg, Mies Edith Lodge, Miss Constance Lodge, and Miss Emily Beecroft, who each wore cream French canvas with moss-green trimmings and hate to matcb. SUSPICIOUS DEATH OF A CHILD.—MT. BrighonFe. coroner, held an inquest at the Fleece Hotel, St. Helens, on Friday, on the body of an unknown child, which was found in a bar in Baldwin-street. on the previous Tues- day.—Elizabeth McCormack, of 9, Fenton-street, said she was passing Mr. Egan's marine stores in Baldwin-street, when she saw a bag on the ground between a cart and an iron pipe, lying -close to the wall of the marine store. She thought it contained rags, but on examining it she found the boar of a child. She communicated instantly with the police, and the body was removed to the public mortuary. She had been past the same place on the previous evening, so that the child could not have been lying there long.— Police Sergeant Gilligan said the child was wrapped up in a rough sack bag, which was sewn up at both ends. There was nothing about the sack that could lead them to identi- fying the person who deposited it where it was foun3. The police had made diligent inquiry for the person who had placed the child there, but they had failed to arrest anyone, although they entertained a suspicion of a woman who was seen in the neighbourhood on Monday evening.—Dr.Masson said be had made a post•mortem examination of the corpse. The lungs floated in water, and from all that he saw he was of opinion that the child was born alive. He did not think •it had lived many minutes. It might have been born on Sunday or Monday.—The Coroner said by the post-mortem examination made by Dr. Masson, they had a simple duty to perform, and that was to return an open verdict, and say that the child died from hemorrhage, but there was not suf- ficient evidence to prove whether or not it had been caused by neglect of any person. Such a verdict would enable the police to take any steps they thought fit. That, he thought, would be the best course to adopc—The jury returned an open verdict.

CRICKET.—The Australian innings cl,sed yesterday for 186; Warwickshire, three wickets for 18. The Central Harbour Union have nominated Mr. Henry George for the office of Mayor of New York. The body of the man who committed suicide on.the Great Northernlway, near Granthani, was yesterday identified as W. Algernon Swain, of Kingsford, Kent. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND THE. TITHE QUESTION.—The Central News Birmingham correspondent, having inter- viewed Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, is authorised to contradict the statement that on his return from the continent he will start a movement for the abolition of tithes. A MOONLIGHT ATTACK ON A POLICE HUT.—A Tralee cor- respondent telegraphs that an attack was made on Thursday night by moonlighters on a police hut near Feale Bridge, about 15 miles from Tralee. The police returned the tire, and shot one of the party, who received a charge of buck- shot in the side. They succeeded in capturing five others, mad brought them into gaol. FIRE AT WOLVERHAMPTON.—A serious fire broke out on Friday morning on the premises of the Midland Electro- plate Manufacturing Company at Wolverhampton. The flames spread so rapidly that in spite of exertions of the fire brigade the building in which the fire originated was entirely gutted. For a time the adjoining buildings, used as a carpenter's shop and dwelliag-houses, were in great danger. THE BELEAST RIOTS —At Belfast, yesterday, Privates Callen and Dysart, belonging to the Black Watch and Lan- caster Regiments, were cbarged with drawing their bayonets on four civilians. The evidence showed that Callen had beela assault.d by a woman, and in attempting to catch her the soldiers were surrounded by a threatening crowd, against whom they had to defend themselves. They were handed over to the military authorities. THE DOD.WO tan MllRDER.—Yesterday, James Murphy, the notorious poacher, of Dodsworth, who is charged with murdering Constable Austwick, was taken before the Barns- ley magistrates. The prisoner, who questioned the wit- nesses in a most cold blooded manner, and contznded that Austwick had injured him, was committed for trial at the assizes ; as was also William Goss, brother in-law of Murphy, for having Larboared the murderer in his house. It was stated Murphy was housed and fed by GOS&OR the 3rd sth. and Tth of August, and on the .6th, Bth, and 15th of September:

FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN AMERICA. Toe American despatches of the 14th inst., landed at Queenstown on Thursday morning from New York, say an :appalling accident happened that day on the New York, Chicago, and St. Louis Railway at Silver Creek, N.Y. As excursion train left Erie with upwards of 1,000, people on board for Niagara Falls, under the auspices of the Methodist Episcopal Church. The train passed over the big trestle at Silver Creek all right, and was just entering the cut on a curve beyond when the engine-driver and his fireman, Harris, descried a train coming upon them from the east. The en- gine was reversed, and the engineer, fireman, and the baggage man jumped' off. In another instaNt the engines came together, were completely demolished, and.the baggage car on the ex- cursion train went crashing through the smoking car, telescoping it from the front to within a few feet of tne rear end. 'I here were about forty people in the car, and the un- fortunate excursionists were eaught and crushed in their seats, which resulted in eighteen persons being instantly killed and :t-fteen seriously wounded. The first movement made was to cut out the sides of the car and to relieve those nearest at hand. The baggage car was also jacked up, he which time surgeons had arrived from Angola. The deed and wounded were moved with wonderful alacrity, and in thirty minutes every body was lying on the top of the hill. The scenes beggared description. Two or-three men had apparently made an effort to escape by the windows, and these were crushed out of all human semblance. The dead were carried into the freight house, where an ingest was to be held as soon as the bodies besides those named could be Identified. The scenes were painful and most agonising. The greater part of the excursionists turned back home panic-stricken.

The Russian Consul is said to have received a telegram announcing that General Kaulbara is the bearer of a Russian ultimatum to Bulgaria. Now that the episode of the legal conspirators is terminated, people are at a lose to understand the real object of the Rbssian ul- timatum. They sappose it can have no other meaning than that Amen has made a compilation of all her demands, and now presents the summary alternatives to the Regency either to accept them or be prepared for the occupation of Bulgaria by Russian troops. div.head: SION MOVEMENT.
div.p: SION MOVEMENT.

Last evening the first of a course of twelve lec- tures on "The History of the Colonies in America," which it is intended to give during • tha• coming winter in connection with the Cambridge Univer- sity Extension Movement, was delivered in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, by Mr. G: E. Green, 8.A., of St. John's College, Cambridge. There was a large attendance. The subject of the present lec- ture was "Systems of Colonisation." Mr. C. BROADBENT, J.P., in introducing the lec- turer, said that the reputation of Mr. Green had come before him, and they all anticipated a very interesting course of lectures on a very interesting subject, and he hoped that on their part they should be able to furnish him with a large and intel- ligent audience. Those lectures had been a source of pleasure and intellectual enjoyment, and he was sure they were glad to once more meet in connec- tion with those University lectures. (Hear, hear.) Mr. GREEN, in the first part of his lectnre,gave an interesting account of the Phoenician; Carthaginian, Greek, and Roman colonisation. Before turning to modern forms of colonisation, he said it should be noted that in every case in which the ancients founded colonies they founded cities, the moderns, they should find, founded states. The reason for the difference was not far to seek. The colonies of each age copied only the models they possessed. The one had lived his life in the city and the other in the country; The Portuguese was the earliest of the modern colonists, and his colonisation was the result of a desire to found a maritime road for commerce between Western Europe and Eastern Asia. When modern Europe was beginning to slr ,vly acquire definite shape, and feudalism to disappear before the rise of nation states, the main 'commerce of the world was that between Europe and Asia. The object of the Por- tuguese establishing colonies was commerce, and not denomination, , and consequently they did not acquire any large extent of territory. They were content to fix themselves in the best stations for subjecting the 'native princes and monopolising the traffic in Europe. It was the defective administration of the Portuguese colonies that ultimately led to their ruin. The object of early Spanish colonisation was the acquisition of gold and silver, the mines of Mexico and Peru being the great attraction which drew the attention of the Spanish kings. Therefore all the early colonies of Spain were mining settlements. The govern- ment of these .colonies was in the hands of the native Spaniards, who were not permitted to settle, and were subjected to a council sitting in Spain. The supreme authority rested with this council, which in turn was solely dependent on the ' king. The Spaniards were noted for the severe restrictions they imposed on intercourse with their colonies which were administered solely with re- gard to the benefit of the mother country. The Dutch introduced a new factor into colonial history —the commercial company, but the Dutch colony at the Cape of Good Hope was an agricultural colony of the ordinary type. The French colonies were of three kinds, the commercial, agricultural, and plantations, of which the latter alone were sue- cessful,largely owing to the privilegesthey enjoyed, the fact that strangers were free to visit and settle there, and the permanent residence of the planters. The English planter hastened to make a fortune and then hurried home, but the Frenah planter, on the other hand, devoted his whole time to his planta- , tion, which he made his home, and at which ho brought up his family. With regard tct, the colonies,

.. however, they could not but be struck with the varying' progress of those of the French and Eng- lish, especially in America. They could not but be struck by tbe apparent anomaly. The French were under the charge of wise and far-seeing statesmen, whilst the English were either left wholly to them- selves, or hampered by senseless interference. Yet while the former decreased, the latter increased. The very neglect of her colonies by England wau. in their favour, for they learned to govern them-- selves, repress their own disorders, and frame their own laws. Thus it was that France,of all European statis of the 17th and 18th centuries, the most I powerful, failed to stand against the enterprise of a little island; inferior in wealth, numbers, and indus- try. In New France nothing that was old and worn was let go, but in New England all was otherwise. There the colonies owed their existence to those theories of religion and civil liberty that were opposed-to the very principles of Ng'w France. There the king was only loved as long as he left the emigrants alone; nobles were few in number, and counteracted by the large class of vigorous farmers; and while in New France there was not one dissen- ter from the dominant church?, in New England men worshipped' iin the forest in their own fashion. England at the outset pursued a liberal commercial policy, which for a time she alattndoned, but only to, return to it again after the diminution of her em- pire. Mr. Green then explained the various sys- tems of colonisation, and concluded by referring to the old colonial system, now happily abandoned. The policy of last century, he said, was dominated by the so-called mercantile sys- tem, a system that started with! the assump- tion that money was of all commodities the most precious. and therefore the most I greatly to be desired. The object was to so manage foreign trade as to.bring more money into a country than went out, and therefore .a nation that suc- ceeded in such a policy obviously did so at the ex- pense of its neighbour. This commercial policy became a cunning game of diplomacy and fraud, and led to national hatreds and wars. In its incep- tion the mercantile system rested upon some slight basis, fOr the systenvof standing armies which was then being introduced needed a long purse to main- tain it. Before they condemned the system, they must remember that' this, and this alone, rendered it possible for Pitt; to exclaim "I will conquer America in Germany:" And in the Phcenician colonies the stranger was sacrificed to the gods, so in the Spanish colonies he was thrown into dun- geons. Fiance, Holland,. and even England fol- lowed in the same' path, and as in the old world commercial interest was paramount in fram- ing alliances, regulating-wrers, and dictating treat- ies, so in the new world'it hampered the growth of the colonies, and yet paved the way to their inde- pendence. It was England that, all unconsciously, gave the death-blow to the old system by absorbing all the colonies, and thus deprived them of their interest in the maintenance; of an exclusive policy. (Applause.)

(Hear, hear.) WESLF.YAN HARVEST FirSTIVAL.—The harvest festival in connection with Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, was celebrated on Sfurday. The chapel was very handsomely and appropriately decorated for the occasion, a great deal of trouble and much in- genuity having evidently been expended to make the interior,of the edifice as fine as possible. The decorative Materials comprised a great variety of fruit, vegetables, and cereal's; and these had been utilised and displayed in the' most effective fashion. The pulpits were graced with strings of snowber- ries, bunches of grapes, ferns, /iliums, and palms; while the communion thbie was so to speak transformed into an autumnal trophy., It was hung with beautiful maiden-hair ferns, and laden with fruit such as melons, peaches, Siberian crabs, and upderneath was an exceedingly well-formed miniature stack and collections of a variety of vegetables. The communion rails were wreathed with moss, relieved with roses, and bunches of grapes and other fruit, and: the windows, pillars, gas bracket s,and other parts of 'the chapel were similarly embellished. The work of decoration had been car- ried out by Mrs. Dutton, Mrs. Cutting, and Miss Stelfox, assisted bya number of ladies and gentle- men. At each service there was a large congrega- tion, especially in the *evening, when the building was crowded. In- the morning the Rev. G. E. Young preached, selecting for his text the follow- ing passage, "He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed. shall doubtless come again rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him." In the evening the Rev. G.E. Cutting preached from the text, "Say not ye there are yet four months, and then cometh the harvest? Behold I say unto you, lift up your eyes and look on the fields, for they are white already to harvest." The collections a the' day, which were mainly- to clear off the circuit debt, amounted to £lsls PARISH CAURCH THANKSOPTING SEUVICES.—The harvest Thanksgiving services were commenced in the Parish Church, Warrington, on Thursday even- ing. The sacred edifiee had undergone an effective decoration with-fruit; corn, wheat, vegetables, Sze, and presented a, most beautiful appearance. The communion table received careful attention from , a number of Indies connected with the Clergy Daughters' Ihstitution, the window sills being laden with fruit, vegetables, and various greens, whilst the wall behind the communion table was artistically set out with floral emblems, promi- nent among whieh were the letters" 1.H.5.,' in the form of a monogram: The supports of the commu- nion rail were nicely bedecked with rushes and' other greens. The pulpit had, been very prettily- decorated with corn, &c., relieved with bands of' red dahlias, gladiehrs, and other flowers. A floral monogram of' the letters " LES. " and several' bunches of 'grapes suspended in front of the pulpit gave the decorations an additional charm. This work was carried out by Miss Jessie Allen. The prayer desk was attractively bedecked with lillies, ' white dahlias, &c., and its appearance, reflected' credit upon Miss Dooley. The front and borders of' the choir stalls were laden with flowers, vege- tables, and' fruit, and evidenced the care be- stowed in the work by Misses Ada and Harriet Chrimes. The Misses Robinson bad spared' none the less pains in the decoration or the clergy, stalls, and the font, decorated' by Mrs. Quekett, wife of the Rector, looked pleasant and attractive. The brass standards and gaseliers and each' of' the window sill's had also receited at- ; tendon,. and they looked' extremely pretty- as result of' the labours of Miss Boyle, MiSs Brooks, !Cgs Hind,. Miss Gittins, and Miss Cassidy. On the walls of the Church seasonable texts were diSplayed. The tablet erected to the memory of the late Mr. Thomas•Eaude had not- been forgotten, two pretty wreaths, worked by loving hands; having been placed on and around the black and' white marble. The services on Thursday evening were hilly choral, and there was a large attendance. The sermon was preached by the Ven: Archdeacon Bardsrey, M.A. The choir rendered the anthem. The injured man said: lam a collier. r know the prisoper. On Satin' davnight last, about twenty minutes to tve Ryer' was stan- ding in the garden in front of this house. At the time there was a disturbance in the road opposite. Prisoner Nyns there. She was fighting with a man and ranniag among, them taking part in the disturbance. She came to where was standing and said "It is-that -- red-nosed devil I want 'to corns out" (meaning Mrs,. Deacle.l She bad a "brat" (apron) on, and some bricks in it. 'She lifted one out and threw it at me. It was half' or threecluarters of a brick: It struck me on the right side of the head and cat it. I fell on the top of the railings. I lost my aenses-- had seen another brick go by me before I fell. When I re- covered consciousness Hound myself-in this bed, and it was Sunday morning: I have been in.bed ever since atter ded by a doctor. I had rot taken any part in the disture turbatsce, and had not given prisoner any provocation. I have been very ill and the doctor said he did not think 1 should recover. A' clergyman has seen me.—Ptieoner -- Did you see me with a "brat,' on.—Yee.—How many were there throwing bricks beside me.--Nobody.—Ptisoner.—gr- Johnston, it is no matter what I say, they are all against ene through a bit of bother. (To the injured man :) Was it not- George downstairs that was raising the bother wa4 out when I went out.—Was he not sghtiog, ?—They'. were all fighting together.—How long have you known nee? —I have only seen you three times at the topof the entry-e-- How could you tell me in the dark ?-.You stood in front of me The Clerk-(to Carr).—You are positive it was prisoner That is the woman.—Alderman Harrisone(to prisoaer).-- Have you anything more to say ?Ptisoaer.—lt is no use asking him anything. No matter what Desk. him, he will deny it.—The injured man made his mark to the deposi- tions, and prisoner, was taken back to the 'Dawn Halle.ana afterwards to Walton Gaol.
